subtopic: STATEMENT BY RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN

speechtext: On the Order: "Questions":

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desired to make a statement with regard to the Prime Ministers' Conference on the Orders of the Day, but I was engaged at the moment. I would like to move to return to the Orders of the Day.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN
speechtext:
Earlier in the session, Mr. Speaker, in response to a question from the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), I gave briefly some of the subjects that had been presented for discussion at the proposed Prime Ministers' Conference to be held in London in June of this year, and I intimated that should the agenda become at any time more complete or definite I would feel it my duty to so advise the House.
Last October I concurred in a proposal made by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom that there should be held not later than June next a meeting of the Prime Ministers of the Empire. Since the last meeting at the Peace Conference in Paris there has been no opportunity for personal and direct consultation between the Prime Ministers on the broad issues of policy in such external matters as may be of common concern. Views were exchanged more than a year ago concerning the holding of such a meeting during 1920; but it was concluded at the time that this would be impracticable; and the same conclusion was reached when, later in the year, one of the other Dominion Prime Ministers suggested a meeting immediately following the first Assembly of the League of Nations. It now appears that the middle of June next is a feasible date for all concerned.
The proposal was made and accepted last October on the basis that the June meeting would be of a special and preliminary character having in view the necessity of discussing-
(1)	Preparation for the special Constitutional Conference contemplated in Resolution 9 of the Imperial War Conference of 1917 to be held at a later date, this pre-

paratory discussion to include such questions as the meeting place, date, composition and agenda.
At the same time it was considered that the June meeting would afford an opportunity for discussing certain other matters of common concern which are of an urgent or important nature, such as-
(2)	A general review of the main features of foreign relations, particularly as they affect the Dominions.
(3)	The question of the renewal of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, which is indeed only a part of the general subject of foreign relations, but which is especially urgent since under the terms of the Alliance a decision should be reached this year.
(4)	Preliminary consideration, preparatory for the proposed Constitutional Conference, of some working method for arriving at a common understanding as to policy in such external affairs as concern all parts of the Empire.
Since that time various other subjects have been suggested for inclusion in the agenda of the June meeting. These subjects, however, in view of their technical character and of the fact that they are not of the same urgency, would seem to belong to the agenda of the Imperial Conference proper whenever its next regular session is held; and since it is very desirable that the special meeting of prime ministers in June-which is not a meeting of the Imperial Conference-should not be of a prolonged character, it seems unlikely that any considerable attention can be given to such questions, which represent an extension of the original programme. The Canadian Government have already expressed a doubt as to the inclusion of some of these questions.
These additional questions, the first two of which were proposed by the Governments of Australia and India respectively, and the remainder by the British Government, are as follows:
(5)	Inter-Imperial communications by land, sea and air.
(6)	The position of British Indians in other parts of the Empire.
(7)	Naval, military and air defence.
(8)	The recommendations of the Overseas Settlement Conference recently held in London.
(9)	The development of civil aviation.
(10)	The reports of the Imperial Shipping Committee appointed as a result of resolutions 11 and 24 of the Imperial War Conference of 1918.	'

(11)	The findings of the Technical Commission appointed to discuss the question of Imperial Wireless communications.
(12)	The question of German reparations, including the division as between the various parts of the British Empire of any amounts received.
(13)	Imperial Statistical Bureau.
(14)	Imperial patents.
In these circumstances it will be seen that the proposed agenda cannot be regarded as a hard and fast arrangement. It seems most likely that no subjects will be discussed that are not included in the above list; but on the other hand it seems most unlikely that all of these questions can be taken up, or indeed, in the view of the Canadian Government, that more than the first four will be closely discussed. Circumstances may develop which will render conclusions desirable on some of the other subjects. In respect of many of them, it would seem that the meeting could do no more than take cognizance of proposals to be considered later.
Later on as the result of the communications that passed between the leader of the Opposition and myself, I agreed that a day should be set for discussion-I think I agreed previously as well-or for an opportunity for discussion to be offered to any hon. members of this House who desired to make observations on the agenda or on the course that the representative or representatives of Canada should pursue at the conference, I now give notice that on Wednesday the House will be moved into Committee of Supply and such opportunity will then be afforded.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN
speechtext: May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question? He has given four subjects which he states have been definitely settled as subjects to be submitted for the consideration of the conference. No one of these four subjects relates to Imperial defence. On the other hand, the Prime Minister of Great Britain has stated in the British House of Commons that the whole scheme of Imperial defence will be considered at that conference. Can my right hon. friend give us any further information as to that subject?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN
speechtext:
No, there is no other information that I can give. It has been placed on the agenda by the British Government. It has been submitted by them as one of their proposals with regard to the agenda, and that, doubtless, is the basis for the statement made by the Prime
Minister of Great Britain. The subjects which I have mentioned will not constitute the full agenda of the Imperial Conference.

That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the unlimited natural resources requiring development in the GaspS peninsula, better transportation facilities should be established at the earliest moment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope I shall not occupy more than twenty minutes in moving this resolution. I have on another occasion described the marvelous natural resources of the peninsula of Gaspe. It is admitted to-day that this large peninsula is one of the wealthiest portions of Canada, from the agricultural, the fishing and the lumbering point of view. There are also in that peninsula traces of oil, zinc, asbestos
and other minerals. The question which I wish to bring to the attention of the House this afternoon, however, is that of railway transportation. I regret that my good friend the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has not arrived from Montreal, otherwise he would have supported, with his usual eloquence, my resolution.
As the House is aware, many years ago a railway was built from Matapedia on the Intercolonial to New Carlisle in the county of Bonaventure, the line hugging the shore of Baie des Chaleurs. The distance is about one hundred miles. Later on the Laurier Government aided, by subsidies, another company which built an additional one hundred miles of line from New Carlisle to Gaspe Basin, the finest land-locked harbour there is in Canada. Therefore^ there are two hundred miles of railway in the peninsula of Gaspe following the shore of the Baie des Chaleurs. Fortunately for the English company which controls both lines, they have had a young Scotchman by the name of Gordon, who has been able, in spite of adverse circumstances, of difficulties and obstacles of every kind, to manage the road most economically, but, of course, the receipts of the two companies are not sufficient to provide a first-class service, and there are loud complaints. To make a long story short, last year, at the request of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), and at my own, the Railway Commission, headed by the present chairman, Hon. Frank Carvell, went to New Carlisle to investigate the whole situation. The investigation took place at New Carlisle under the chairmanship of Hon. Frank Carvell on April 8. They were to investigate as to the character of the service, the condition of cars, the lack of cars, the cancellation of a passenger train three times a week, thus reducing the service to a tri-weekly service. The grievances of the public can be summarized as follows:
1. The railways have not given a daily mail and passenger service each way between Matapedia and Gaspe. 2. The railways should be ordered immediately to purchase first-class cars, steam-heated and lighted, at least with gas. 3. The Government, not being disposed to acquire those railways, should see that the companies be ordered to ballast their line. 4. The companies should be ordered to make the following improvements and reforms: Replace ties and also rails when necessary; construct new bridges where required; cut down the grades; acquire locomotives that would haul the ordinary tonnage as on other

roads; build proper workshops and acquire proper tools so that the men working at the engines might be able to do efficient work; erect proper fences along the whole of their line; build additional water tanks; provide sidings at the various stations; build sheds large enough to hold the merchandise which is very often exposed to the weather for lack of space; haul empty cars from Matapedia so as to take care of the outgoing freight; dig drains and cut weeds; acquire facilities for loading live stock; sweep the stations once a day and keep them clean; and make some arrangements to keep the mails under cover at Matapedia, the mail bags now being left on trucks and often left outside over night.
This is a brief summary of the complaints made against the railway company. The patrons of the road have suggested two alternatives in case the company would not reform itself-either to put the company into the hands of a receiver, or to have the Government add this 200 miles of line to the National railway system. The Railway Commission sat for a day or so and investigated all the grievances which I have summarized. Be it said to the credit of the company, it was found that in many instances the complaints were somewhat exaggerated. On the whole, it was found that the company was doing its best, with limited financial capacity, to meet the requirements of the public from a passenger and freight point of view. A good deal of evidence was given as to the financial situation of the company, and their statements show that the Atlantic, Quebec and Western Railway Company, which represents the last one hundred miles of the railway, had made in six years a total loss in operation over gross earnings of $245,375, and that the Quebec and Oriental Railway Company, the old Gaspe railway, during the same period had made a net gain of $182,788. But the company, through its able manager, Mr. Gordon, contended that all of this money had gone back into the road in the way of betterments, and I think that the chairman of the Railway Commission and his fellow workers found that this statement was true.
I need not go into all the figures. I will quote simply the concluding paragraph of Mr. Carvell's judgment on the whole situation after the investigation. He said:
Generally speaking. I found the road-bed from Matapedia to New Carlisle better than I had expected, although it was far from what might be considered an up-to-date road-bed. All the rivers and larger streams were spanned by steel bridges of light construction but still in fairly

good physical condition. The rails are 56 lbs. to the yard, but evidently of good quality, and the track well laid. The new ballast was quite evident in many places, and there seemed, to be a reasonable number of new ties added within recent years. Culverts were in many cases very deficient, station houses dilapidated, and the whole road showed unmistakable evidence of financial stringency. The passenger cars are antiquated and should not be used for first-class passenger traffic on any railroad. The engines were light, many of them old. and no doubt very expensive as to maintenance. In fact, I do not think any railway company could hope to carry a large amount of traffic, either* passenger or freight, with the equipment now in use on these roads.
A vast amount of evidence was given to the amount of business available along the Gasp6 shore. However, generally speaking, it may be summarized as follows: There is a population of 75,000 with no other means of communication with the outside world by rail. They, of course, to some extent, can carry on business bv water. The fishing industry alone amounts to over $2,000,000 per year. There is a large pulp and paper mill at Chandler on the Atlantic, Quebec and Western. There are enormous forest reserves extending north into the interior for many miles all along the line. The agricultural possibilities are considerable, but nothing like what could be produced were better transportation facilities provided.
As a result of our negotiations, the daily train to Gaspe was restored on May 1, and I have heard no complaints about it up to the present time. The passenger equipment is antiquated and only fit for second-class passenger traffic. They require at least Wvo modern, first-class coaches and one chair car to accommodate the business, and, in my judgment, they require at least four modern locomotives, which will take care of the passenger service. They also require an up-to-date machine shop for the purpose of effecting the necessary repairs to equipment, and I see no possibility under the present financial condition of the company of these necessary improvements being provided, unless they can rent the use of some from either the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National Railway, and, as the traffic is entirely with the Canadian National, it would seem to me to be a good business investment on the part of the latter road to furnish this road with the necessary equipment, both locomotives and cars, at a very reasonable rental.
That is the gist of my proposal to the Government. We do not ask-and I say "we," because I speak on behalf of my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and myself-that the Government should take over that road; the Government has already enough lame ducks in the National Railway system. But it seems to me that we are quite reasonable in asking the Government to treat generously this important feeder of the Canadian National railways. I say it is an important feeder; that is admitted by the Chairman of the Railway Commission. Mr. Gordon, the manager of the road, who has won the compliments of the commission, states in a memorandum

which was addresed to the Railway Commission in the month of February last:
The fact should not be lost sight of that wo are responsible for supplying the national railways, without cost to them, traffic yielding in revenue something like a million and a half dollars per annum. Inquiry into this should reveal the fact that we are extremely valuable feeders, and, I think, it was to the interests of the national railways to see that we continue as such and that we get every reasonable assistance so we may be able to develop and encourage traffic by continuing such rates in effect as the traffic can stand.
All we ask from the Government is that it implements the suggestion made by the Railway Commission that some of the equipment of the Canadian National railways be rented, if not loaned, to this company, in order to give it a chance to pass over the peak of its difficulties, that is to say, over this period of hard times. We do not want the Government to put the company under the'hammer. We do not ask the Government to take over the road as a lame duck, but we do ask the Government to give this important feeder of the Canadian National system a chance to function, and a chance to develop, by lending to it a few locomotives, a few first-class cars, and a few freight cars. We are not asking anything beyond the recommendations of the Chairman of the Railway Commission. We will be satisfied with that and so will our electors.

I notice that the hon. gentleman stated that the rails were 56-pound rails, and that he complained that the locomotives on this road were not modern. Would it be possible for the heavy locomotives that are used on the Intercolonial, for instance, to travel over this road with its 56-pound rails?

I would not think so,
but I think on the Intercolonial and the Canadian Northern they have smaller locomotives in their old equipment, which would be quite acceptable for this line of railway.

The road is not in a
receivership ?	,

Oh, no. In closing I
express the hope that the Government will look into this matter and give it its best consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways, to
whose department this definitely appertains, is not in his seat to-day nor in the city. However, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) is perfectly justified in going on, as this will be the last day for
159J
private members. Yet the difficulty of adequate reply to the very able presentation which he has made is enhanced by the absence of the minister.
I can only say this: Assuming, as I do, having no reason at all to controvert any of his assertions, that there is much in the case that the hon. member presents, it is only on a par with very many other parts of the country which are also suffering considerably for lack of local transportation advantages. The difficulty of catching up with transportation needs in Canada is very great; great by reason, first of all, of the overbuilding of transcontinental lines, resulting in part in financial obligations at the present time that make it unusually hard to meet local needs such as this one. The financial situation generally is such that the Government, in justice to the country and the country's future, has not been able to consider favourably proposals which ordinarily would strongly appeal as being good business investments from many standpoints. I can only say on behalf of the minister and of the Government that the case presented by the hon. member is well worthy of consideration at the earliest possible date, and that consideration will be given to it. I know of the importance of the peninsula and the importance of the county. Its importance is such that I know any hon. member would be proud to represent it, and I can assure ' my hon. friend from Gaspe that what he has said will be taken into consideration at the earliest possible date.
Mr. ,LEMIEUX: I have only to thank the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) for the favourable consideration he promises to take of the case. I shall send to the Minister of Railways the memorandum containing the investigation proceedings held by the chairman of the Railway Commission and the statement made by the manager of the company. The demands and suggestions are very modest and, I think should receive the most favourable consideration from the Government.

That, in the opinion of this House, a more efficient train service for both passengers and freight should he established on the Transcontinental Railway between Winnipeg and Quebec.

He said: Again I shall be as brief as possible. This matter may appear somewhat sectional, and in a way it is; but the country is so large that it is quite difficult to visualize from one point the whole extent of its territory. My resolution asks that a more efficient train service for both passengers and freight shall be established on the Transcontinental railway between Winnipeg and Quebec. As my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) knows, the Government of the province of Quebec has, for about ten years now, been giving very considerable attention to the settlement of that area known as the Abitibi district. This district is immense; the timber reserves are enormous, and it is situated in the famous Clay Belt. The district is especially attractive to our French Canadian settlers in the province of Quebec, and already, through the beneficient influence of the Minister of Agriculture in Quebec, as well as of the Minister of Colonization, the province has been able to contribute from the old parishes an army of some 15,000 young settlers, who are all established between Cochrane and Quebec at various points on the Transcontinental line. Some years ago, that territory was but a "great lone land;" to-day there is quite a development in process. There is particular development in the pulp industry and in saw-mills. There are magnificent water-powers. And, what is even more important than all this, the settlers on the land are able to grow wheat and are anxious to duplicate in that territory the old province of Quebec itself. Now, I do not wish to launch a discussion on the question of freight and passenger rates; I shall confine myself only to the necessities of the district. Though the people are provided with a splendid railway line in the Transcontinental, they find that the rates at present are a very serious impediment to the development of the region.
Is this territory now included in the province of Quebec?

Yes, and it is represented in the House of Commons by my hon. friend the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). His county extends from Timis-kaming up the Transcontinental including Amos and other points. The province of Quebec has divided into townships or cantons the whole of the Abitibi region, and I shall be pleased to send to my hon. friend the last report of the Department of Colonization in Quebec on the progress 
made by the settlers there. Indeed, it is something remarkable. As I was saying, the question of rates is the most vital one for the district at present. I know it is equally vital elsewhere, and again I ask the indulgence of the House if I confine myself only to that district.
The reason why I bring the matter before the House is that I happen to know very intimately a man who, though he may be young, may properly be called the father of the region. Indeed, he is its factotum. I refer to Mr. Hector Authier who, one might almost say, selected the site of what is to-day the prosperous town of Amos. He is president of the Board of Trade, he is mayor, he is agent of Crown lands, and he may very well be described as the live wire of the district. He is above all a patriot; he has been going into the old parishes of the province of Quebec and inducing young men to establish homes for themselves in that beautiful country of the Abitibi. And he has succeeded. That district produced last year 100,000 cords of pulpwood and 50,000,000 feet of timber; but, as Mr. Authier writes me, this could be considerably exceeded if there were a proper train service with fair rates. The district is not as well known as it should be. The Quebec side comprises upper Timiskaming, the Abitibi proper, and the basins of the Harricana and the Nottaway rivers. Mr. Authier states- and he is sustained in this opinion by the surveyors and land agents of the Quebec Government-that there are ten million acres of good land fit for cultivation and colonization in the Abitibi. Sir, if at times some people feel blue about the future of this country, let us remember that we have the settlers who constitute our greatest asset. Let us help them by giving them proper facilities and in being fair to them in the matter of rates. The soil which they till enfolds tremendous possibilities. The future of this country lies in its farms. The land is the great asset of Canada. Let us get as many settlers as possible on the land, and the country will take care of itself. In the Abitibi, says Mr. Authier, there are ten million acres of land fit for culture where the Canadians of French descent will thrive and prosper if they are given proper facilities and some encouragement. Now the Transcontinental-and again I am speaking only of that section of country- the Transcontinental, which is a first class line, unequalled in any country in the world, would pay if you first settle the country. The land is there awaiting the

settler. But when the settler has reached the land you must give him fair rates on the railway and provide him with a service worthy of the name. The population, as I stated a moment ago, in the Quebec end of the Abitihi, is fifteen thousand people. It is increasing in spite of the adverse circumstances I am about to describe, and Mr. Authier, who is the factotum of the district predicts that in ten years there will be one hundred thousand Canadians from Quebec located there.
Now I will, in a few words, summarize the gist of the grievances of those hardy settlers. First, says Mr. Authier, we have no cars, or very few of them, and the locomotives are poor. Our timber is being piled up at the stations. That increases the insurance costs and practically discourages and diverts traders from our district. Second, our timber being piled up at the stations because of the lack of cars, in the summer forest fires will destroy that good timber thus piled, and that is another cause of discouragement to the traders of the district. And then there are the excessive freight rates. At present the settler, Mr. Authier says, makes a living out of pulp wood. That gives him a chance, . or rather a breathing spell, until he has cleared his land. Mr. Authier gives some of the rates in the following column:-
From Amos to La Tuque 17 cents per 100 pound, or $8.50 per cord.
From Amos to Grand'Mere 21 cents per 100 pounds, or $10 per cord.
From Amos to Three Rivers 23 cents per 100 pounds, or $11.50 per cord.
From Amos to Hawkesbury, Ontario, 22 cents per 100 pounds, or $11 per cord.
From Amos to Temiskaming, 25 cents per 100 pounds, or $12 per cord.
From Amos to Thorold, Ontario, 32 cents per 100 pounds, or $15.50 per cord.
From Amos to Corinth, New York, 27 cents per 100 pounds or $18 per cord.
From Amos to Watertown, New York, 39 cents per 100 pounds or $19 per cord.
As regards sawlogs the rates are:
From Amos to Quebec 25 cents.
From Amos to Montreal 31 cents.
That is from $7 to $10 per thousand feet in the first case and if $9 to $12 in the second case.

Who
made those rates?

The Railway Comission. However, I am not discussing that feature of the matter in detail. I suppose it will some day form the subject of a special debate. I am only citing these few cases to show the Government the
absolute necessity, if we are going to maintain those settlers in those far away districts, of considering the railway rates and giving the settlers special consideration in view of the peculiar circumstances in which they find themselves. I appeal to the Government to kindly look into this matter, and remedy the situation at the earliest possible moment. Mr. Authier is very optimistic as to the future of that district, and it is well that we should have optimists at the present time in our country. In order to remedy this situation, and to maintain the tide of colonization and settlement to that district, here is what he suggests :
We should be able to ship timber from Amos to La Tuque for $4 per cord ; to Grand'MS re for $5 per cord ; to Three Rivers, Hawkesbury, or Temiscaming for $6 per cord; to Merritton or to Thorold for $7 per cord ; and to Watertown or to Corinth, for $9 per cord.
He is quite frank in stating that he understands the rates throughout the whc'.e country must be such as will give the whole railway system a chance to live. He admits that frankly, but he claims that there .are particular problems for particular districts and that those special circumstances should be considered by the Government. It is true that in the present instance this district is along the lines of a transcontinental railway, but for that district the Transcontinental plays the part of a colonization road. Therefore the Government should act in a broad way in this matter, and give what I would call "the most favoured nation treatment" to these settlers. They are the most deserving portion of our population.
I will not say anything further. I think I have in these few words set up a fair claim for the favourable consideration of the Government. By all means, Mr. Speaker, let us stand by the settler. I remember the campaign, started some years ago by Mr. Rider Haggard, of "Back to the Land." That movement, if it is in the least aided and sustained by the Government, may, after all, solve many of our troubles in the future.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac) : Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) in bringing before the Government the difficulties and some of the grievances of the people of the Abitibi district. Perhaps the greatest grievance they have with regard to the passenger service is that the trains are not being operated in a way to best serve that settlement. It is five hundred miles from Quebec to La Reine,

and from Nottaway to La Reine, taking in the whole district westward, there is a settlement of about one hundred miles. This settlement, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Maisonneuve, consists now of about 15,000 people. There main support in the early stages of settlement is .pulp and lumber. They take out pulpwood for dealers along the line, to be shipped out to the mills in the different districts. When the settlers went in there the rates were not much over half what they are to-day, and consequently they were able to ship out their pulpwood at a profit, but since the last rate increase it costs something like $3.50 to $4 a cord more to take out the pulpwood. This practically makes it impossible for the settlers to get any returns from what used to be a very profitable source of revenue to them.
This is the system of settlement in Quebec. The Government allows each settler one hundred acres of land at a nominal price, and he starts to take out his pulpwood. He is allowed to cut a certain area in the first year-about ten acres, the next year another ten acres, and each year he must clean up the land and put it under cultivation before he cuts down the next ten acres of pulpwood, so that his land is under cultivation long before he has exhausted his timber resources. In addition to getting his land under cultivation he must also build a house and do certain settlement duties. In that way, as the pulpwood is cut off, a good farming district is being developed. I spent some time there in 1917, 1918, 1919 and 1920, and there has been a marvellous change in that time. The country is very much like Western Canada, with the exception that it is covered with commercial spruce timber. The land is very level, the soil is clay and very productive and will maintain a large number of prosperous settlers once it is cleared up. But unless those settlers can utilize the pulpwood as they go along it will be impossible for them to get the land under cultivation.
The system in Ontario is the opposite. There the timber is cut without any settlement regulations, and any hon. member who has travelled through that country knows that as soon as he passes La Reine station, which is the boundary between Ontario and Quebec, the country westward is practically a wilderness. The timber has been cut off and the land not left in fit condition for settlement. As a matter of fact, settlers will not undertake to clear up the land of timber that is not commercial.

As the hon. member for Maisonneuve has stated, there is a settlement in that district of 15,000 people, and they claim that that one hundred miles of settlement will take care of the fixed charges and operating-expenses of the railway for a distance of four hundred miles down to the next main division where there is another settlement. But under the present conditions it is just possible that if the freight rates are not decreased these people will have to move out of that settlement, for, unless they are able to sell their pulpwood and lumber it will be impossible for them to make a living. The high freight rates also discourage new settlement. As has been pointed out, there are millions of acres of land fit for cultivation in that country. And it is peculiarly adapted for settlement with the least possible railway facilities, because there are watercourses every few miles along that portion of the settlement between Nottaway and La Reine. I do not think there is more than ten miles at any place where there is not a considerable navigable stream crossing the tracks, and the country is so level that navigation is easy against as well as with the current. That allows of settlement along the rivers quite a distance from the railway as the settlers can transport their products by water to the railway.
The people in that district complain of the passenger service. The train going westward leaves Nottaway, which is the first village in the settlement, at 9.43, and a local train leaves at 10.10, only about forty minutes later. Those trains continue to Amos and O'Brien with only that short interval of time between them. Amos is the largest town in the district and is the banking centre. The land office is also located there.
Have they two trains a day?

One mixed train and a through passenger train, but both running at practically the same hour. The train coming back from Amos arrives there at 2.27 in the morning and as it is very often late it is a hardship to the people there to have to reach their destination in the night time. The arrangement may be all right for through traffic, but it could not be possibly worse for local traffic. It makes it almost impossible for the people to travel except by staying over from one day to the other.
What is the distance?

Between the two main
points it is 112 miles, and the train going east runs through that territory at night. There have been complaints about the freight service ever since I have known the district, and that is since I. became a member of this House. I have repeatedly seen the Minister of Railways and the officials of the Department of Railways and Canals to try and get an improvement in that service. The people in that territory two years ago had their pulpwood out and could have sold it provided they could get freight cars. It was then selling at about $7 a cord. But many of the settlers were obliged to sell at $3 and $4 a cord because they could not get cars to ship it out, and no person would pay any higher price for the wood under those circumstances. The dealers simply paid what they liked for it. They could not hold the wood until they coud get cars and get a better price; therefore they sold to the speculator at whatever price they could get. That has been the condition for the last four years in that country. Last year when they wanted cars they could not get them. When I went up there last June they were getting $16 a cord for what they call burnt peeled wood, that is, wood from areas over which fire had run so that the bark came off easily. To-day that wood is not worth more than $7 or $8 a cord, and they lose the difference because they could not ship the wood out. It simply means that settlers who have gone in there with the expectation of making a good living have become more or less discouraged and in turn their friends with whom they are corresponding are also deterred from going in, so that settlement is being retarded. Fifteen thousand people will practically take care of that line from La Reine to Quebec; if there were thirty thousand people in that settlement the line would be making a nice profit and would help to carry other portions of the road. If these people move out of the territory it will be almost impossible to get others to come in, at least for many years, whereas if good railway facilities are offered to the people and if the rates go down in the near future so that they can ship their wood out, you will have a very prosperous settlement in that country.
I have spent some years in Western Canada and in new territory throughout the country and it seems to me that the new settler always gets somewhat the worst of the deal. When the railroad is first
built into the district it is usually operated under the direction of the contractor, who has the privilege of charging whatever he likes. Then when it is put into operation by the railroad company they give the worst possible service-that is, they give as little service to the territory as possible. This is very discouraging to the people at a time when they need encouragement. Most people when they move into a new territory have not a great deal of money or they would not be there. They are generally young people who are going in to make a new home for themselves. If they are not allowed to get out their product and sell it and therefore do not prosper in the territory in which they settle, they are apt to be up against it all their lives. If these people had better facilities and could get cars when they wanted them, then they would be able to get a good price for their wood and they would be prosperous; but the condition to-day is that-the merchants in the territory are carrying many of the farmers who have taken out wood. The tracks are piled with wood for practically one hundred miles-all along the track there are thousands and thousands of cords of wood that could not be shipped out when the price was right and cannot be shipped out now on account of high freight rates. It is very discouraging to the settlers, and if there is a remedy it should be found at once in order to encourage settlement in that district and make the operations of the railroad there profitable, thus bringing about benefit to the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this matter should properly be brought to the attention of the Canadian National railways. When last year or the year before we incorporated the Canadian National Railway Company it was understood that we were going to take these railway matters completely out of politics. In fact, they are supposed to be out of politics now. It does seem to me that the Liberals in this House should be the very last to want to-
Improve the service?

Not to improve the service, but project this whole' question again into the political arena. If the districts to which reference has been made require better service, the matter ought to be brought to the attention of Mr. Hanna and his highly paid officials. I understand that Mr. Hanna is in receipt of $25,000 or $30,000 a year-I have no doubt he is worth it-

and that other members of the staff receive proportionately large sums. What is the use of having such a high-salaried staff and such a complicated system of management if those who want to increase our railway facilities may not present themselves to these gentlemen and ask for those improved facilities? These men who are managing the Canadian National railway are railway men-at least, I hope they are; and they would be very quick to see that a district of this kind should be properly served and given adequate railway facilities.	'
I am not suggesting what Mr. Hanna should or should not do, but I live in Montreal and I know something about the Canadian National trains that leave that city every day for Ottawa. We have a Canadian National train-Grand Trunk-that leaves Montreal at four o'clock every afternoon, and we have also a Canadian Pacific train leaving at the same time. Then we have a five o'clock train on the Canadian National, going through the very same country. I understand that we have also another train leaving Montreal for Ottawa earlier in the day. It costs the Canadian National, we are told, one dollar and twenty-four cents for every dollar they make. It seems to me that if there is such an urgent need for railway service in the semi-explored country to which reference has been made, it would be a very simple matter to divert some of these trains to that district, where we plight possibly make money, instead of running them from Montreal to Ottawa. Now, with regard to the Canadian National train which leaves Montreal daily at five o'clock in the afternoon-I believe it is the Trans-Canada train-we know when it leaves, but the Lord Himself only knows when it arrives in Ottawa. It is a de luxe train, everything of the best; no train in the country can compare with it in appointments and makeup; yet quite often it arrives in Ottawa an hour and a half late. And its late arrival is not a matter of infrequent occurrence; it happens almost daily. I do not say that it is always an hour and a half late, but it is all the way from twenty, twentyjfive or thirty minutes up to an hour and a half late, in some cases even two hours. When we ask the officials why this train is late we are told that the train has a number of hot boxes on board. Well, I do not know what hot boxes are; I never saw any of them; but if we have hot boxes on board and they keep us late, why not take those hot boxes off and travel without boxes at *Mr, Jacobs.!
all? Now, the Canadian Pacific train is never late. We have these competing lines with trains leaving Montreal for Ottawa at four o'clock. The Grand Trunk will have possibly two or three passengers on board, all non-paying guests, while the Canadian Pacific train is filled, and sometimes you cannot get a seat. The reason is that it is known when the Canadian Pacific will reach Ottawa.
People do not seem to like "de luxe."

It looks like that. Now, I would be opposed to any "favoured-nation" scheme as proposed by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve and Gaspe, (Mr. Lemieux). He thinks that his particular district should be put in the favoured class because the people there are pioneers. Well, it seems to me that every one who is on the land and trying to earn a living is a pioneer. The people in the West are pioneers just as the people in the Abitibi country are. After all, the people who are in that country do not require hourly communication with metropolitan centres; if they go up there they must expect to endure some hardships, otherwise they are not good pioneers; and they must make the best of it until sueh time as we are able to put these roads into a little better shape than they are at present. When Lord Shaugh-nessy's scheme is adopted we may be able to give them all the facilities they require. But it seems to me that this matter should not for the present go beyond the extent of an academic discussion. We all feel that every person in the country should have proper railway facilities, but on the other hand we also feel that we are running practically on to the shoals of bankruptcy if we continue very much longer in the way we are doing. It seems to me that the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe, while he may be enthusiastic about this particular region in the Abitibi country, should first of all consider the general needs of Canada. If he does that, I am sure that he will realize that the time is inopportune to advocate for that district any better system than pioneers have in other parts of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I were to attempt to reply to the case presented by the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) and the other two hon. gentlemen who followed him, I would have to imagine myself first as the chairman or other member of the Railway Commission,

and present such considerations as from their standpoint could be advanced against the suggestion contained in the motion. The motion, while it reads quite innocently, is clearly intended, as shown by the speech of the mover, to he an appeal for lower freight rates on the Transcontinental in so far as that road serves the Abitibi district-
Better car facilities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-and better car facilities as well. That is a subject which, by the legislation of this House, in, I think, the year 1903 or about that time, was placed definitely and exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. Both phases of the purpose sought by the resolution, the car-provision phase and the rate phase, are definitely assigned to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission; not only is this so, but the Railway Commission, in its conclusions, in its conduct of cases presented and the disposition thereof, has been placed, by the legislation of Parliament-and wisely so-in the statuts of a judicial tribunal; and it seems to me, in the discharge of their duties, they are consequently not subject to the review, either by way of criticism or defence, of members of the House of Commons or of Parliament. Consequently, I really am not quite able to grasp how Parliament could well deal with the resolution as presented this afternoon. The subject of railway rates having been so assigned and the tribunal being supreme, subject, of course, to appeal to the Governor in Council in the regular way, and subject to the responsibility of the Governor in Council, in disposing of an appeal, to the Parliament of Canada, it does not seem to me appropriate or wise that we should occupy the time of Parliament in the discussion of the correctness of rates or maxima fixed applicable to various districts or divers commodities. If we do, we are simply going back to the position in which we were before 1903, and we are doing a great deal to reduce the authority and usefulness of the tribunal to which all those questions were assigned. If Parliament is to act and to adopt any policy as regards railway rates, Parliament would be justified in asserting in the Railway Act provision for discriminatory rates favourable to this or that class of commodity or this or that kind of community. If Parliament found it wise to place such a direction in the Railway Act-and I think Parliament would1 be very reluctant to adopt that course-then, of course, the Railway Commission would be compelled to take cognizance of the
direction of Parliament as contained in the law. But unless we choose to act in that way, it seems to me that we are absolutely bound to leave under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission the prerogatives that are there by virtue of legislation, and not directly or in any other way to seek to bring those back into the forum of Parliament for discussion. I say this, not with particular reference to this resolution, but as a general principle, in the desire to impress this principle not only on members of Parliament, but on the country generally. There has been for some time throughout the Dominion a disposition to regard the Railway Commission as merely the instrument of the Government of Canada to do the will of the Government in respect of this application or that, in respect of the disposition of this question or that, and to hold the Government responsible for each and every act of the commission, just as if it were a department of Government doing the will of its master.

They have enough sins
without putting that at their door.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If sins were to be
attributed to the commission, I do not think that would be done by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux).
No, the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government having roamed so long without having any sins brought home, it would be really a pleasant variety if the hon. member could succeed.
The practice of which I have spoken has become more or less prevalent of recent times, and I take this opportunity of saying that the more it grows and the more it is encouraged, the worse it is for the usefulness of the Railway Commission and, in my humble opinion, for the Dominion of Canada; because I think it is of first importance to this Dominion, not only that the sphere of responsibility be conserved to the commission, but that its status be carefully observed and that throughout the Dominion, people understand that that commission is not an instrument of Government but in every respect a judicial tribunal with certain stated and highly important powers.
I have said so much in that regard. If I were to argue whether it would be wise on the part of Parliament to insert in the Railway Act the principle that special rates should be allowed in serving pioneer districts, if I were to answer the case presented from that standpoint, I would say

this, that I fear the line of division between what is a pioneer district and what is not would be very hard to find, and interminable difficulties would arise in deciding just when a district ceases to be a pioneer district and becomes an established territory. The claims of Abitibi would certainly not be alone. I can think now not of one district but of a very large number of districts in this country that would immediately claim to enjoy any advantages that might be granted to this particular district, and others that had been denied them in days gone by would ask to be recouped for what they had suffered, so that complexities that would be very hard to get over would immediately ensue. Parliament is wise, in the interest of all concerned, to leave this to the commission and to hold the commission responsible for the discharge of its duties, just as any other judicial committee or board is held responsible.
As to the general subject of railway rates, this in its general aspect is under the commission too; but all of us will agree, without criticism one way or the other, that the sooner we get such conditions that a general reduction can take effect, the better. There is no question that the present rates-and I do not deny that they are necessary, I do not deny that the exigencies that have been brought upon us and by which we are surrounded make them necessary-there is no question that the present rates are such that they are a serious deterrent to the commerce of this country, and while certain causes must be remedied or improved before there can be any substantial reduction, the sooner those causes are removed or remedied the better for this country. We see the' effects every day, and the object of this country and of this Parliament should be to direct its efforts to removing the causes rather than to complaining of the consequences.
I have every sympathy with the settlers of the Abitibi district. I happen to have been there, and I know some of [DOT] their handicaps. Insofar as it is a question of railways rates or car supply, it is a question for the disposition of the Railway Commission. If the Government is at fault in not providing sufficient car supply for our own railways, at the request of the directorate of those railways, that is a charge which we must take care of and for which we must be responsible. But I do not think that that will be alleged. 1 think the Government has gone, up to the present, as far as it could be justified in going in meeting the requirements of the
[Mr. Meighen.J
railway directorate for car supply. Consequently, a charge of neglect cannot successfully be laid at the door of the Administration.	.

I, do not wish to prolong the debate, but as the question of rates is under discussion on this resolution, I might be permitted to say a word or two. . I quite sympathize with the remarks of the hon. member who introduced the resolution (Mr. Lemieux)
I think that the settlers of the Abitibi region have certainly a grievance. There is no doubt that products are brought over that road from thousands of miles west at the same rate per hundred weight as these settlers have to pay for their pulp-wood to go to Quebec, and the only reason I can assign for that is that the Railway Commission when it undertook to hoist the rates, just went at it blind and made a general increase all over the country. As a result business has been stifled; business is really at a stand-still to-day in Canada, and unless something is done to ease the rates and remedy present conditions I do not know where we are going to come to. The railways have their sidings piled up full of empty freight cars, because it does not pay anybody to ship over the roads. Our railways and our shipping were going to do great things for us, but what is the result? The freight rate from Toronto to China is about $27.50. That is about $2 more than it is from Chicago to China. The rate from New York, Montreal, or any of those ports, to China, is fixed at $20

1That is the American rate. The American rate for ocean freights is entirely based on a law which passed through Congress compelling ships to take certain crews and pay certain wages. They cannot charge less from New York to China than $20. The pre-war rate was $8.50. The same tonnage is carried on the ocean for the came distance at prewar figures to-day from Great Britain, Germany and France, and the result is that they are getting all the foreign trade., I cannot understand why this country cannot get somebody on the commission who has a little brains, and will endeavour to adjust the freight rates so that the people of this country can do business. It is a most shocking thing to know that freights have been raised in the last six. months or the past year to the point where we are entirely out of the foreign market. It is no use having ships on the ocean if you cannot compete. We have to compete with other countries with our products,

and our ships are tied up by the American rates. If you ask for a rate in this country, the first thing they do is to look up the Pittsburg rate and hand that to you. That is all nonsense. We should not be tied up to the American rates at all, and as long as we do remain tied up to them, we shall be underground all the time and this country will not succeed.
The only thing to bring relief to this country is an early reduction of taxation and of freight rates. When we get that, we are going to get back to business. If the present rates are to continue I have no hesitation in saying that inside of a year not one-quarter of the equipment of our railways will be in use. We have all read what Lord Shaughnessy said in the paper this morning about amalgamating the roads. That is not going to affect the rates at all. It is no use sending a man into the woods up at Abitibi to cut pulp-wood if he is going to make a loss of 50 cents a cord when he gets it to the station. People must be allowed to make a living.
I suppose that for the western farmers the increased rates have meant an additional ten or fifteen cents a bushel out of their pockets direct, and nobody seems to be the better off for it.
I am very glad that the hon. member for Maisonneuve has brought this matter up so that hon. members are able to say a word or two upon this very important question. I want to tell the right hon. the Prime Minister that unless something is done to enable us to get through rates of freight over the government railways to foreign countries, instead of having to pay two local freights, and fifty per cent more than any other country has to pay, outside of the United States, we shall have to close up business. We have had a foreign trade in manufactured goods in Canada amounting to close to a billion dollars. I have no hesitation in saying that instead of that trade showing an increase, it will show a falling off next year of fully fifty per cent. The whole thing is due to the rates, to handing over to two or three irresponsible clerks the making of the rates for the whole country. I say that Parliament must be responsible to the people of this country for the management of the large affairs of the nation, and the sooner we realize that the better. I do not approve of bringing every little matter into this House, but there are certain general questions that we must discuss, and one of them is the condition of the railways
in Canada and how we are going to get out of our present trouble.
The British Columbia lumbermen are in exactly the same position as the Abitibi settlers. They were seeing daylight last fall. The price of operation had fallen and reductions had been made so that they were able to reach busines in the East, which would have enabled people to start building operations but the very minute lumber could be delivered in Ontario and the East at $50 and leave a profit to the lumberman, that very minute the commission hoisted the freight to $17, which shoves lumber out of sight, so that there is nothing in it for anybody. It is a pity the commission say they have to do it. What should actuate the Railway Commission is a study of conditions in Canada, instead of trailing after the American idea constantly. We are trailing after the American idea in everything, in the hoisting of wages and the hoisting of rates. Now everybody knows very well that in Canada, with our tremendous distances, we cannot exact the same ton-mile freight as they can in the United States. If the Canadian Pacific Railway had endeavoured to exact the same ton-mile rate as was exacted in the United States, its road would not be in as grand a position as it is in to-day. There is ample earning power in all our railways here. The only thing that is needed is to give the people a chance to do business at a profit. It is no use putting the freight rates up so high that everybody doing business is going to lose money. The lumberman in British Columbia or Abitibi starts in to cut his lumber and carry on his operations, and when he gets through he finds that all his profit has gone and that he is indebted to the railways. That is no way to do business. There must be more elasticity.
This idea of making a judicial body of the Railway Commission is only a method of giving the railways a chance to squeeze the public more than they should on freight rates. The idea of the average railway man or the man on the commission is to charge all that the traffic will bear. That will mean absorbing every dollar that everybody in this country makes, whether in the factory, on the farm or elsewhere, and if you are going to carry on like that you will have a poor country. No one will come here and establish factories and do business unless conditions are just as favourable as in any other country. I am glad to approve of the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. COMMONS
Lemieux); so far as he is concerned, I think those remarks are directed in the proper channel. As regards Ontario, I think the slashing down of pulpwood areas applies only to certain regions handed over to the pulp companies. The Government has assigned certain territories to these companies, who virtually own the land and are supposed to have the right to cut wood on these territories for hundreds of years if they desire; but where there is a settlement in Ontario, they carry on business much the same as in Quebec. There are enormous areas in northern Ontario beyond the Height of Land and beyond that again there is a territory along the basin of the Albany river that would accommodate a population of a million. There is plenty of arable land there and hardly a white man from Ontario has ever set foot in that district. We do not know the extent of our wealth and resources.
We have been building railways and now we must see that they are operated so that not only they themselves will profit but that the people of the country will be benefited. There is danger in giving them a free rein in the way of high freight rates and thus shutting them off from business, because if they charge too high rates they will not get business. The point of the whole matter is to reach some adjustment whereby goods can be carried at a profit to all concerned; the railways should not get all the profits any more than the producers. I trust that this matter of freight rates and the general situation will be further discussed in the House before long, when we shall have an opportunity of going more thoroughly into the matter. The member for Maisonneuve, I presume, does not intend to press his resolution.
I shall not detain the House at any length.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must direct the attention of the House to the circumstance that the mover of the resolution is about to close the debate.

I have no apologies to offer for having brought this question to the attention of the House, notwithstanding what my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), has said. My hon. friend belongs to a race which for centuries past has been persecuted and denied the enjoyment of freedom. But we belong to a free race; we recognize that Parliament is our forum, and when a man is denied his rights it is the duty of any public man to bring the matter to the

attention of the Government and of the country. Now, it has occurred to my hon. friend to have certain grievances aired in this House that might well have been referred to special departments. I have in mind, for instance, the case of some poor Jewish immigrants who were denied the right of entry at Quebec and Halifax, and my hon. friend was very glad to take the opportunity, when he could not get justice from the department, to air his grievances before Parliament. This is the forum of every free man, whether he be Jew or Frenchman, or a representative of any other race.

Mr. JOHN A- CAMPBELL (Nelson) moved:

He said: For fifty years the question of the ultimate control of the land and other resources of that immense district known prior to 1870 as Rupert's Land and the North West Territory has been before the people of Canada. This question arose when these vast regions were handed over by Imperial Order in Council to the Dominion, and Manitoba became a province, and it is a very live question at the present time. That the problem should still be before us after half a century of controversy is due to the fact that it was approached in the first place from the standpoint of expediency instead of from the standpoint which must ultimately settle the question, that of right. Even now the question of expediency seems to prevail in the counsels of those who have to do with the matter; the constitutional rights of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are continuously being ignored.
The present situation is somewhat anomalous; I have had occasion to mention this at different times in this House. Unquestionably it is the view of Canada generally that these resources will eventually be handed over to these provinces. Just when that will be is pretty hard to say, but in the meantime what is the situation? There are some matters that demand immediate attention. Laws should be passed in connection with certain of our natural resources. I might refer specifically to mines and minerals; The minerals in the provinces alluded to are under the control of the Dominion but there is no mining law in existence. Yet the conditions are such that it is absolutely essential, in the interest of the proper development of Western Canada, that a comprehensive law should be enacted. The Dominion declares that as these resources are going to be handed over to the provinces action in this respect should be deferred. The payment of the £300,000 was thus occasioned not by the transfer of Rupert's land to Canada, for that was effected, it will be seen, by full cession from the Crown; it was exacted by the Hudson's Bay Company as a sine qua non for the surrender of their charter rights in Rupert's land.
It may be stated at once that scrupulous regard for sound British constitutional procedure was observed throughout the difficult process of transfer, and that the implications of that procedure leave the British principles with regard to self-governing communities- and above all, with regard to Manitoba which was entrusted with provincial status from the first-in full force and operation.
The transactions to which I refer were two. The first was the surrender by the Hudson Bay Company to the Crown of all their interests in the two territories mentioned, and the second was the cession by the Imperial Government, by Order in Council, of these territories to Canada.
I might also mention here that there seems to be a popular delusion that all of this territory which was transferred by the Hudson Bay Company to the Crown, is in the West. As a matter of fact, perhaps most of the territory is not covered by the provinces to which I referred, but now forms parts of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There was never any question raised as regards those two provinces as to the control of their natural resources. Naturally, in a constitutional way, the beneficial interest in the lands and natural resources of the territories now included in Quebec and Ontario became vested in those provinces, and these provinces continue to exercise jurisdiction and control over them.
The treatment meted out to Manitoba and the other western provinces is in direct contrast to that shown to British Columbia and Prince Edward Island at the time that they came into Confederation. In 1849, the Hudson Bay Company was granted certain rights over Vancouver island, rights similar to what they had over Rupert's land. In 1867, however, the Imperial Government decided that it was in the interest of the colony that 
those rights should be relinquished, and an arrangement was made whereby the Imperial Government should pay to the Hudson Bay Company a certain sum for the relinquishment of all their rights in connection with Vancouver island. This sum, amounting to £57,500 was paid by the Imperial Government to the Hudson Bay Company for the cancellation of the rights of that company in Vancouver island. In this instance, however, Great Britain did not retain in any way the lands or natural resources of Vancouver island, but the administration thereof was handed over to the authorities who subsequently took control, not only of Vancouver island, but of the mainland which subsequently became the province of British Columbia.

In connection with British Columbia, at the time that province came into Confederation, 100,000 acres were set aside for the building of the Canadian Pacific. The

agreement with British Columbia was that 100,000 acres should be transferred by that province in trust to the Dominion to be used in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The important point, however, in connection with this territory is that the lands were to be transferred to the Dominion in trust. The consideration was that the Dominion should pay $100,000 anually for those lands, and this sum was paid from the time the province came into Confederation, notwithstanding the fact that the lands themselves were not transferred to the Dominion for ten years after and the railway was not built for five or six years after that.

The ultimate aim of the Confederation appeared to be to extend the territory from the West to the Pacific ocean, the idea being that other provinces should be formed out of this territory and be admitted to Confederation from time to time. The idea of the Imperial Government was not that these provinces should be admitted at any time at all, but that their admission should be held off until they had shown themselves capable of self-government, and that they should then be admitted as selfgoverning entities. However, the Dominion of Canada in 1870 arranged that Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories should be admitted, and that part thereof should be formed into a province to be known as the Province of Manitoba. So in this case the Government of the day was acting illegally in two respects; (1) in that it had no powers to form provinces out of the territories taken ovejr, and (2) in that the British North America Act did not contemplate that the lands of the provinces would be otherwise administered than by the provinces themselves. So the land clauses in the Manitoba Act, as pointed out by Mr. Thompson, disjointed the whole constitution. The crowning iniquity in this connection was the enactment in 1872 of the first Dominion Lands Act, whereby it was declared that the lands and natural resources of the West-it was Manitoba that was referred to at that time-belonged to the Dominion. No title in the Dominion was revealed by that Act. The fact of the matter is, and this is contended by constitutional authorities, the Dominion Government never had any title to these lands, but was simply acting in the capacity of trustee for these lands and natural resources. In effect, it was in the position of loco parentis to the territories over which it exercised jurisdiction, and the taking over of the lands of these territories meant that the povinces which were formed out of them became simply geographical areas, and were not provinces in the same sense as the other provinces of Canada were.
The history of the contention of the West for the control of natural resources is rather interesting. As I have already pointed out, the lands were taken by the Dominion Government, in the first place, without a suggestion being made of any subsidy being granted to Manitoba; that was the only province formed at that time. Thus Manitoba was restricted as in its

possible sources of revenue. One reason that was given for the appropriation of these lands by the Dominion was that they would be required for the purposes of immigration in connection with the great immigration policy which the Dominion Government had in mind at that time. This did, however, for some time work to the disadvantage of Manitoba. The influx of immigrants made it necessary that roads, bridges and other public works should be constructed by Manitoba, and as site had no lands which she could could sell, and so raise money to defray the expenses of these public works, she found herself in a precarious position financially, as a result of the policy followed by the Dominion Government. In 1882 the situation became so serious that the Hon. John Norquay and a delegation came to Ottawa and placed the facts before the authorities here with a view to securing some satisfactory adjustment. They requested a subsidy in lieu of lands that had already been alienated by the Dominion, and asked that the residue of lands should be turned over to the provinces. The only result of this trip to Ottawa was the agreement on the part of the Dominion to grant $45,000 annually to Manitoba, as in the case of Prince Edward Island, in lieu of lands. However, as I have already pointed out, the situation in connection with Manitoba was entirely different from that of Prince Edward Island. The point to be emphasized is that the $45,000 was granted under what were supposed to be circumstances analogous to those that existed in connection with the grant to Prince Edward Island; that is to say, it was given in lieu of lands which had already been alienated. Subsequently, in. 1885-I	shall not
go into details-the grant was increased from $45,000 to $100,000, being the same amount as in the case of British Columbia, previously referred to.

Mr. Speaker, just before the House rose at six o'clock I had read a letter written by the premiers of the three western provinces to the right hon. Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of the Dominion, dated December 1913, wherein were set out the intentions of those provinces regarding the transfer from the Dominion to them of their natural resources. This letter was written, as I said, at the request of the Prime Minister in order to establish a basis for negotiation betwen the Dominion and the provinces. It did not necessarily follow that the premiers who signed that letter would insist on those terms being carried out absolutely. When people enter into negotiations they generally prepare their case with the idea that there will probably be some modifications, and that a conclusion will be reached somewhere between the contentions of the parties to those negotiations. It was largely with that idea in view that the provincial premiers wrote this particular letter, although I am satisfied they thought they were not asking any too much even if the terms of that letter were carried out implicitly. Nothing in the way of conferences or negotiations appears to have taken place in connection with the matter from that time until the year 1918 when a conference was called in the latter part of that year by the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden.
Strange as it may appear, not only were the western provinces called into conference at that time, but the conference was thrown wide open to all the provinces of the Dominion. In a word, the Prime Minister said to the other provinces: "We are going to do something for the western provinces in the way of handing back their
resources which I promised to give them when I should form a Government, and this may be a good time for you to get into the game and possibly some benefit will accrue to you through these negotiations." Naturally the other provinces were only too glad to take advantage of the situation, and when the conference met they preferred claims as to the additional subsidies which they contended they ought to receive in the event of the lands and resources of the western provinces being restored to them. In other words, the fiduciary responsibilities of the Dominion regarding the western provinces should be settled according to the fiscal expediency of the other provinces. It is unnecessary to'point out that no satisfactory solution of the difficulty could be arrived at in that way, and so nothing resulted from the conference. It passes my comprehension, Mr. Speaker, why the other provinces were called into this meeting at all in view of contentions which I have already advanced and which I will elaborate a little later. A further conference was called last year, and representatives of the provinces met here toward the end of the year. The case for the western provinces was submitted by Manitoba. I have a copy of it in my hands, but as that case has already been presented to the Government I shall not do more now than read an extract or two therefrom. But first I want to point out that in the case as presented for the prairie provinces opportunity was taken at the outset to withdraw thfe letter of the provincial premiers to which I have just referred. This was done for specific reasons stated as follows :
This proposal-
That is the proposal of the premiers to which I have referred-
*-'was dictated by the desire on the part of the provinces to accede to the request of the Canadian Government for joint action in submitting "a proposal which would serve as a basis for negotiations." The widely varying conditions and development of the three provinces, seemed to make absolute similarity of treatment upon any other basis impossible. The misconceptions, however, of the proposal of December 22, 19,13, though in the opinion1 of the Prairie Provinces unwarranted, have been such as to make the withdrawal of that proposal advisable at the present time.
And the contention of the Prairie Provinces as set out in the case submitted last December is summed up in the concluding paragraphs as follows.
We beg: to submit that any permanent settlement of the "natural resources question" must be based upon the ample recognition on

the part of the Dominion of the inherent British rights of the Prairie Provinces to their natural resources as from the date of provincial organization or responsible governments; the restoration to full provincial -beneficial control of those which remain unalienated, and compensation upon a fiduciary basis for those which have been alienated by .'Canada "for the purposes of the Dominion."
It seems to me that case is clearly and specifically set out there, and that until this principle is conceded-a principle which should never have been in doubt at any stage of the game and one which is clearly and distinctly embodied in constitutional practice and history-the negotiations cannot have any successful result. If that principle is conceded, subsequent negotiations will have reference only to matters of detail and should be settled, with satisfactory results, without delay.
I desire to make a further remark or two regarding the alleged interest of the other provinces in connection with this question of the natural resources of the West. I do not know upon what ground the other provinces claim to be interested in any way in this matter-presumably it can only be as members of the Dominion. If it is as members of the Dominion then they can have no such claim because, constitutionally, the Dominion has no right to these resources. This is explicitly shown in clause 109 of the British North America Act which I have already quoted. If any commentary on this is needed I have it in the statement made by the hon. Mr. Monk when this matter was under discussion in the House a number of years ago. The interpretation given by him would appear to be constitutionally correct and should certainly meet with the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite. On the occasion referred to Mr. Monk said:
The interpretation given hy the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upon section 109	.	.	. has always been favourable to the provinces, and has gone very far in the direction of maintaining that all public lands .... once the province is created, fall under provincial control .	.	.
By common understanding of section 109 and the interpretation put upon that section since our constitutional questions have arisen, it would seem to be evident that public lands, by the very terms of the constitution, belonged to the provinces the moment they entered Confederation, and I see no reason for departing from that rule in regard to the province created out of a portion of the Northwest Territories.
In a word, the other provinces had no more interest in the lands and resources of these western provinces, and had no more right to compensation for their alienation or for their transfer back to those to whom

they rightly belonged, than Great Britain had not only in Vancouver-to which I have already made reference-but in the whole of Canada, as was pointed out emphatically by the present right hon. member for Kings (Sir Robert Borden).

As to the wisdom of these three Prairie Provinces having handed over to them the public lands is a question between the Federal Government and the provinces interested and affected, I do not wish to express any opinion in relation to that question.
It would seem then that the matter is absolutely one between the Dominion and the western provinces, and that their respective governments should get together and settle it. If any of the other provinces have any grievances they should be taken up in the same way.
