It has been said that the western provinces not only want their lands but their indemnities also-that they want to have their cake and eat it. A certain amount of money has been given to the western provinces since 1882. I wish again to emphasize the fact that during the first twelve years of the history of Manitoba not only did she not have her lands, but nothing was given to her by way of indemnity in lieu of those lands. But the statement is not correct that the provinces want not only the money but their lands also. In confirmation of this I need only quote from the Manitoba Free Press, which undoubtedly speaks for the whole of the West.
We have received a large amount of money in lieu of these lands, which is an offset against this asset. On the other hand, there has Ibeen an enormous alienation of part of this national domain for purposes of the Dominion, and this constitutes an offset on the other side of the ledger. A (balance should he struck (between these two accounts and the natural resources

should be transferred to the western provinces, subject to the acceptance of the balance on these accounts by which every party to the dispute is liable for it.
From this quotation it will be seen that the statement as to the western provinces . asking for their lands and their present indemnities as well has no basis in fact.
In the case as presented to the Dominion by the western provinces last December the contention in this respect is as follows:
It is conceded that in applying this principle due consideration must he given to the sums already paid by the Dominion in "lieu of lands" and the cost of administering the lands in the interests of the province, but we are strongly of the opinion that nothing whatever is to be gained at this stage by discussing details until the principle outlined above is unreservedly conceded.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to submit the resolution which was drawn up by western members last year. They met in conference to discuss matters in connection with the natural resources and other affairs of interest to the West. A special committee was appointed to bring in a report on the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces. As a result a resolution was brought in by this committee which was composed of the hon. members for Kootenay, Lethbridge, Battle-ford and Nelson, and was passed unanimously by the conference. The important clauses in the resolution are as follows:
The question-
Which we are now discussing.
-is solely one between the western provinces and the Dominion. The Dominion Government is possessed of all the data in connection therewith and is in the position, and is the proper party to work out and present to the western provinces for aceptance, an equitable scheme or proposal for the transfer to these provinces of natural resources of said provinces according to the promise made to them by the Prime Minister.
Therefore, your committee recommend that representations he made to the Government that it is imperative in the interests of the country as a whole, and particularly with reference to the development of its natural resources, that the question of the ultimate control of the natural resources of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba be settled immediately, and that the Government take the necessary steps forthwith to have this done.
The resolution emphasizes the fact that the question is one between the Dominion and the western provinces solely, and that immediate action is necessary. It does not state what action, but there can be only one satisfactory and conclusive action

the transfer of these resources to the western provinces on an equitable basis. It is ten years or more since most unequivocal
promises were made in this connection not only by the leader of a great party, but by the party itself. These promises have not yet been redeemed. We ask this Government what they propose to do about them. Surely at this late date it is not asking too much that the transfer of their natural resources he made to the Prairie Provinces without further delay.

Mr. Speaker, the question which my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Campbell) has brought before the House in this resolution is one of long standing, and one that has been considered at different times by successive federal governments. It is not too much to say that it is a question of large national importance. More than one-fifth of the area of Canada is affected, and the importance of Western Canada as a portion of the Dominion has long been recognized. Indeed, that importance is growing every year as its population increases and as its wealth production and its progress in other respects develops.
There is no doubt that the three prairie provinces consider they have a real grievance in the withholding from them of their natural resources, by the Federal Government. They consider that their autonomy as provinces is restricted, that they are not in a position of equality with other provinces, and they think as members of this great confederation they are entitled to be placed in that position of equality. Nothing else but a recognition of that fact will satisfy the people who dwell in that portion of the Dominion. It is rather a striking circumstance that this difference in status should exist when we consider that, for instance, the little province of Prince Edward Island, with a population of one hundred thousand or less, occupies a status in respect to its public domain that the great province of Saskatchewan with a papulation of over eight hundred thousand does not enjoy. The significance of that fact alone must bring itself home to the consideration of hon. members in this House.
But let me give other illustrations. For instance, Nova Scotia has 247 square miles of coal area, all of which it owns and administers in every way for the benefit of the province. Any beneficiary interest there is in the coal mines of Nova Scotia belongs not to the people of the whole Dominion hut to the people of Nova Scotia. On the other hand the great province of Alberta, which is further removed from the seat of government of the Dominion

than Nova Scotia, has, it is estimated, 25,000 square miles of coal area, all of which is administered solely and wholly by-the Dominion, for the purposes of the Dominion, the province exercising no control and getting no direct benefit from its sale whatever. The same is true of our mineral rights. The northern portion of Ontario is rich in mineral wealth. The people of Ontario have control of their whole mineral rights, their nickel, their gold, their silver; whatever minerals may be found there are absolutely within the control of the province, administered for the benefit of the people of that province, and the other portions of the Dominion have no right whatever in them. But Manitoba, adjoining Ontario for hundreds of miles, almost equally rich in minerals-for there are vast mineral deposits in the northern portion of that province-has no control whatever over those resources, since they are held and administered by the Federal Government, as I have said, for the people of the whole Dominion. The same is true with our forest resources and our water-powers. Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick have entire control and ownership of their forests and their timber resources generally. The western provinces have not that right. Every acre of pulp land in Manitoba or Saskatchewan or Alberta is administered by the Federal Government for the purposes of the Dominion; it is not held and administered by the people of those provinces, as is the case in the other provinces of Canada.
It may be said that good reasons existed in 1870, the time of the creation of the province of Manitoba, for not handing over to that province the control of its natural resources. It must be borne in mind that at that time Manitoba had a very small white population, probably not more than ten or twelve thousand souls all told, and some argument can be advanced in favour of the action that was then taken. It is worth while noting in passing, however, that it was taken against the protest of the people of Manitoba, who held when their territory was being erected into a province that their natural resources lying within the province should be under provincial control, as was the ease in other provinces. But, I say, something may be said for withholding them at that time, owing to the sparseness of the white population and the fact that a comparatively small area was under consideration. But the withholding of those resources ought now to be regarded as in the nature of a trusteeship to be 
exercised during the formative period of the province.
Again, in 1905, when Saskatchewan and Alberta were carved out of the vast Northwest Territories, this mistake was repeated. I have always held, and there are thousands in Western Canada who hold, that a mistake was made at that time. As a matter of fact these provinces were starting out; they had.no revenues of their own and they agreed to the proposal made by the Federal Government that they should accept subsidies in lieu of their land. I wish to point out, however, that that arrangement has never been acceptable to a great portion of the people of these provinces and should be corrected without further delay.
The fathers of confederation did not contemplate that we would have two distinct kinds of provinces in Canada. They did not contemplate that we would have one set of provinces with absolute control of the natural resources within their bounds and another set of provinces with no such control. There can be no dispute as to the difference in this respect or to the fact that it exists. The older provinces of the Dominion are sovereign provinces so far as the administration of their natural resources is concerned. In 1912 when the matter of the extension of the boundaries of the province of Manitoba was under consideration in the House of Commons, Mr. Thomas White, afterwards Sir Thomas White, in discussing this matter gave frank recognition to this fact. He said on that occasion, when the matter of subsidies was under consideration:
All the provinces of Canada with the exception of iSaskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba were made sovereign provinces and the lands belonging- to the Crown were vested in these provinces. The result is that they have had the advantage of their lands, their minerals nad the royalties consequent thereon. But this is not the case with the three Prairie Provinces^ They have no -land

 They are not sovereign states in that sense, as the other provinces were, and the result is that prima facie they should be entitled to the same treatment.
That is, in respect to the matter of subsidies. It is, of course, the right and has always been the right of the Federal Government to control the navigability of rivers within the various provinces. There is perhaps a sound reason for that, arising from the fact that streams are very often interprovincial in their character and it is desirable to have the central authority control the powers of navigation on these streams. But that has never applied in the older provinces so far as water-powers and

other water rights are concerned; yet the distinction does exist as between the older provinces and the Prairie Provinces of the West, since the latter have no control a't all of the power rights, or for that matter any other rights in their streams.
Now, it is an interesting fact that British practice, as was clearly pointed out by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) in the excellent review of this question which he has just given to the House -British practice invariably has been that the colonies wherever situated have been entitled to and have been given the right to administer their natural resources. It has always been conceded that the beneficiary interest in the resources of a district or a colony belong to the people of that district or colony, and the public domain has always been surrendered by the Crown for the benefit of the people living in such colonies.
That is true in respect of British colonies throughout the world. Take the case of New Zealand, Tasmania, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and West Australia, to quote examples. In every one of those cases the right to control their natural resources within their boundaries was given to them at the time they were given self-government. If we come to a consideration of the older provinces in Canada, we find the same principle applied by the British Government. In 1840, when the Act of Union took place, the new provinces of Canada, that is, Upper and Lower Canada, were given absolute and entire control of the natural resources within their boundaries. The same was true of New Brunswick and the other Crown colonies in British North America. The Act of Confederation followed this principle identically, and when the Confederation was formed of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in 1867, the right of those provinces to the entire control of the natural resources within their boundaries was not in any way interfered with and was recognized fully and completely. The same thing was true of the province of British Columbia. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) has pointed out, what was the fact, that the province of Prince Edward Island received exceptional treatment from the Dominion in that regard. Its natural resources had already been alienated at the time it came into Confederation, by private sale when it was a Crown colony. With the assistance of the Dominion, that province was able to buy back its natural resources, and it has administered them ever since.
We have had the claim advanced by the other provinces that they have a proprietary interest in the natural resources of Western Canada, and my hon. friend has quoted Premier Murray's view in 1914. That view however, has somewhat altered. I wish to read an extract from the St. John correspondent of the Financial Times, dated November 20, 1920, in relation to /this question. The extract reads:
However the people of Ontario and Quebec feel about it, the governments as well as the people of the Maritime Provinces are determined to press their claims for the financial compensation for the immense natural resources already handed over or proposed to be handed over to the western provinces. At the last session of the Nova Scotia Legislature-
That was the session prior to November 20, 1920.
-the following resolution was passed unanimously: That the province of Nova Scotia urge upon the Federal Government the immediate and just settlement of four matters: Compensation for the lands reserved for school purposes in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan; compensation for the cash subsidies paid to the three western provinces in lieu of lands; compensation for the lands granted Ontario and Quebec, and compensation for the unfair treatment of public expenditure since Confederation.
That is a pretty healthy list of grievances. Premier Murray, in his election address to the people of Nova Scotia prior to the last provincial election, also gave voice to the same view. He stated then:
At the last session of the legislature a resolution was passed calling- for an early conference with the governments of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in reference to the claim of the Maritime Provinces against the Federal Government with respect to Western Lands and the cash subsidies paid to the western provinces in lieu of lands. I deem this matter of the very highest importance and shall press our claims with the utmost vigour for a' readjustment of the federal subsidies on such a basis as will give to Nova Scotia a fair compensation-
Now, note this:
-'for the alienation of vast territories in which our province has a proprietary interest.
That is a very frank statement of the view that the eastern provinces have a proprietary interest in the natural resources of Western Canada. That view was also advanced by the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec in the conference called by the Federal Government in 1918 in respect to this matter. We had this spectacle upon that occasion, of the rich provinces of Ontario and Quebec, with their great natural resources which they absolutely control and administer for the people of those provinces,

to be hereafter established, or by any m"nicipal corporation therein.
Next was the feature that imposed the heaviest burden on the West in this respect.	.
And the lands of the Company in the Northwest Territories, until they are either sold or occupied, should also be free from such taxation for 20 years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
As a matter of fact, 20 years from the grant from the Crown was considered as 20 years from the time the patent was taken out; so much of these Canadian Pacific lands are not yet being taxed in Western Canada, and this has imposed a very real burden on the people in many communities in the West where one can often find several sections of land in a single municipality that pay no taxes at all, thereby placing a heavy burden on the people of the municipality in carrying on their school and municipal operations, and the general conduct of their public business. There is another consideration. It is not too much to say that the opening up of the West brought great prosperity to Eastern Canada. There is no doubt about that. Prior to 1896, or shall I say 1900, the factories of eastern Canada were not running overtime, but after the nineties, and in the early years of the present century, when population began to flood in from the outside world, attracted by the cheap lands of the Prairie Provinces, business was created for eastern industries. The factories in Ontario and Quebec were working overtime to supply the goods required in the Prairie Provinces, and I am quite safe in saying that the Prairie Provinces in the early years of the present century afforded the best possible market for the industries of Eastern Canada. Now, the West takes the position, in this matter, that the other provinces of Canada have in right no equity in the natural resources of the Prairie Provinces, and they feel that this principle should be frankly recognized by the Federal Government and this Parliament. The question has arisen as to subsidies. Subsidies have been granted to the western provinces in lieu of lands that have been withheld from them; but the West is not asking to-day that these subsidies must necessarily be continued upon the present basis if the resources are transferred. They would, I believe, be satisfied that an account should be taken upon a fair basis of the value of the resources already alienated, and that the subsidies to be paid hereafter shall be based upon the value of the lands and [Mr. Crerar.}
resources alienated for the purposes of the Dominion, keeping in mind, also upon a fair basis, the services rendered by the Dominion in their administration. I know that that position was not taken by these provinces a few years ago. This question has been the subject of a good deal of political manoeuvering, perhaps both provinciality and federally; but, at any rate, I think that this suggestion offers a fair basis of settlement of the difference between the Federal Government and the western provinces in this respect. Concede the principle that they are entitled to their natural resources and adjust the matter of compensation that shall be given them in lieu of the lands that have already been alienated. It may be argued that that is a very difficult and impossible thing to arrive at, that the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments cannot agree upon that question. Well, surely some method can be found, either through the friendly processes of arbitration, or possibly by reference of the matter to the Exchequer Court; and have the actual amount payable to the provinces in lieu of lands alienated determined in that way. It should not be a difficult matter to adjust as between the Dominion and the provinces; but the Prairie Provinces will never be satisfied until there is a frank recognition of the fact that they are entitled to their natural resources, and they are placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of the Dominion in every other respect. It has also been urged by the Maritime Provinces that they are entitled to additional subsidies from the Dominion. I have no quarrel with that position if they desire to take it. If they# have a claim in equity against Canada they have a right to have it recognized; but our point is that that has no right to be involved with the question of the transference of the natural resources to the Prairie Provinces. If Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick think they are entitled to additional compensation by way of subsidy from the Federal Government, let them go to the Federal Government and settle that question; but let it be settled irrespective of the natural and inherent right of the western provinces to their resources. That is the position that Western Canada takes. It does not want to do the eastern provinces an injustice; all it asks is fair play in the settlement and adjustment of this question.
I will not further take up the time of the House. Let me say in closing that

the matter of government in the Dominion of Canada is made more difficult because of the vast extent of our country, and the tendency for sectional feelings to develop, as well as difficulties that may arise from other differences. In the interests of harmony in the Dominion, and in order to have a satisfied and contented West, it is necessary that the discrimination in this matter-because the West feels it has been discriminated against-should be removed. Let us take away the sense of injury and wrong that exists there and we will promote happiness, welfare and good fellowship between the provinces of the Dominion.

The ground has been quite well covered by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Campbell) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) but I desire briefly to emphasize a couple of points in connection with this question. The resolution asks that the western provinces be given their natural resources; there is no reference to subsidies, financial terms, or matters of that character. I feel that the attitude of the two great political parties in this country at the present time is an admission that the western provinces are entitled to their natural resources. The former government, led by the present member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) was committed to the return of their natural resources to the western provinces, and at the convention of the Liberal party held a couple of years ago, a plank was included in their platform admitting that the western provinces were entitled to those resources. In both cases, however, there were qualifications, and I think that it is those qualifications that will prevent the western provinces from obtaining their natural resources. My judgment is that the Federal Government should assume responsibility for granting the natural resources to the western provinces, and then if there are any adjustments to be made as regards financial terms or subsidies, it could be done later. I would say that the present Government and the existing official Opposition both admit that the western provinces are entitled to their resources. Then, why not give them those resources and settle other differences afterwards? In my opinion, if the matter is left, as at present, to settlement by the provinces, through their representatives, ' sitting down at a table and trying to come to an arrangement, there will be no settlement whatever. There will always be one
or two provinces that will stand out for better terms and will not consent to those that may be agreed upon by the other provinces. In that way we shall not be able to arrive at a settlement of this very important problem. I think it has been established that the western provinces, from the consideration that has been given to the historical facts of the matter, are entitled to their natural resources. All of the provinces in the Dominion, except the Prairie Provinces, possess their natural resources. Now, one of the provincial premiers, Premier Murray, of Nova Scotia, has been quoted this evening. I saw a statement in the Winnipeg Free Press the other day that Premier Murray, in 1913, in a communication to the then Prime Minister, declared that the question of the wisdom of giving the western provinces their resources was one between the Dominion Government and the western provinces. I believe that in that respect he is right.
I believe that he is right in that respect, that this is a question purely for the Federal Government to decide, and that if there are other questions, relating to subsidies or better financial terms they are susceptible of treatment at a conference between the provincial representatives. I believe that the Dominion should take full responsibility and decide whether the western provinces are entitled to their natural resources or not. Until they do that,' there can be no satisfactory settlement of this question.
Now what does this mean to the western provinces? Take my own province. Probably the only homestead area of any large extent that we now have is in the country to the north of the city of Edmonton. That country was opened up for settlement by the Dominion Government. People have gone in there in recent years and taken up homesteads. Traces of oil have been found in the northern section of the province of Alberta and there are also great timber resources there. The people who have gone in there to open up the resources, and the settlers who have gone in to take up homesteads, had to have facilities provided for them. They had to have roads, bridges, schools and also railroad facilities. The responsibility for opening up the country and bringing settlers in rested with the Dominion; but the responsibility for these other purposes lay with the province; and the province of Alberta, as a result, has undertaken great liabilities to provide transportation and other facilities for the people who have

gone in there. In spite of that, however, they are getting nothing whatever from the lands. They do not own the lands; the Dominion owns them and gets whatever revenue is derived therefrom.
Take the question of the coal resources of the province of Alberta. As has been pointed out, the coal resources there are as great as in any other province of the Dominion, if not greater. But those coal resources are in the possession of the Dominion and the royalties derived therefrom go to the federal power while the cost of the administration of the coal mines of Alberta rests with the Provincial Government. They provide inspectors and they have to provide other facilities for the districts where these mines are established. Yet the Provincial Government derives no benefit from that source. Again, if oil is discovered in Alberta new responsibilities will be imposed upon the Provincial Government, but no revenue will come to them from these resources. Naturally, the people of the western provinces, who are affected, feel they are not being- treated justly, they feel that there should he an immediate settlement of this matter and that it should be. settled satisfactorily to them.
Mention has been made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) of the fact that criticism is offered on the ground that the West has been an expense to the East. The people who criticise the West in its demand for its natural resources, and claim that they should share in those natural resources, forget that they have been sharing in them and are doing so at the present time. All the revenue that comes to the federal power from lands, timber, and minerals in the West is shared by the other provinces, it is not confined to the western provinces. It is true that the Dominion itself inaugurated an immigration policy to populate these western. provinces, and that hundreds and thousands of people have in consequence gone into that country, but those people are an asset to the Dominion as a whole and not merely to Western Canada. What they pay in taxes, either direct or indirect, is apportioned throughout the whole Dominion, it is not confined to the western provinces, and so these people are an asset to the whole of Canada.
I recollect a speech that was delivered in this House, in a previous Parliament, by the then member for Brandon (Mr. Aikens) now the Lieutenant Governor of the province of Manitoba. He dealt with the

argument that the West had been an expense to the East and he met the argument by quoting figures for the financial year ending March 31, 1913. He gave the figures for all classes of revenue from the western provinces, and he also gave the figures for all classes of expenditure. He also gave the expenditure that was solely for the West and the expenditure that the West shared in as a province of the Dominion and he showed that in one year the West provided, by nearly $8,000,000, more revenue than the expenditure upon that part of the Dominion. He went further to show that if the customs figures at the head of the lakes, at the Pacific ports, and a certain share of the customs revenue in other ports of the Dominion which the western people were bound to share in some proportion, had been recognized and credited, the western provinces would have had a surplus to their credit of nearly $18,000,000. But the point I wish to emphasize is this statement by the then member for Brandon on April 17, 1914:
The Government of Canada have received from the sale and leasing of Dominion lands over $42,583,162. They have expended something in respect of surveys and necessary expenses of sale and the like of that, which would be paid out of the ordinary receipts from Dominion lands. But I venture to say that the $42,583,162 received from the public domain in these three prairies provinces will not only pay back what was paid to the Hudson Bay Company, $1,460,000, but will also pay for the whole administration of that domain with interest.
That was the statement of the then member for Brandon, and I think it combats the argument so frequently advanced that the West is an expense to the balance of the Dominion and that the other provinces should share in these natural resources. Let me make another point, and I am merely referring to these figures for the sake of refuting the argument that the West is not bearing its proper share of the expense of the Federal Government and is more or less an expense to the other provinces. I do not happen to have the figures in my possession at this moment, but I recollect the statement being made during the present session. The request was made for information as to the amount of income tax that had been paid by the respective provinces, also the amount that had been paid in income tax by the farmers of the respective provinces. I think altogether about a million dollars had been paid by the farmers of Canada, and of that sum no less than $900,000 had been contributed by the farmers of the three western provinces. I think that proves that the

men who have settled on the western plains, the men who have taken up homesteads and purchased lands there, are bearing their share of the taxation of this country.
This may be, and no doubt is, a difficult problem to settle so long as that settlement is left to a round table conference of provincial Premiers. I feel that this Government can only satisfy the demand for the return of the natural resources by assuming the full responsibility of giving those resources to the western provinces. It is admitted that they are entitled to them. The leader of the previous Government admitted that fact. The platform of the previous Government-I would not like to say that it applies to the present Government because I have not looked over it during the last few months to see whether the present Government gave recognition to the plank or not-but the platform of the previous Government and the platform of the present Opposition admit that the western provinces are entitled to their resources. If that is true why are not those resources given to the western provinces? Why not abandon the proposition that there should be a conference of the representatives of all the provinces and an agreement reached by them? Because that is an impossible proposition; the other provinces will not agree to what / is proposed and consequently the western provinces will not get their natural resources. Give the western provinces their natural resources, and then if there is any difference of opinion as to financial terms or subsidies, take up that .problem afterwards and settle it. Consider afterwards the amount of land that has been alienated and the amount of money that has been advanced to the western provinces as subsidies since they were created, and make some adjustment to settle the matter. Then there will be greater peace and harmony in Western Canada touching this particular question.
Probably the Prime Minister will speak on this question and will state his position and the position of the Government, but I believe that if I interpret correctly the correspondence that took place between him and the Acting Premier of Alberta within the last two months, the Prime Minister still adheres to the view that a settlement must be reached at a round table ' conference rather than by the Government assuming responsibility for giving the western provinces their natural resources. I say now, as I said before, that I do not think it will be possible to satisfactorily
settle this question on any such conditions.
It has been established to-night, I am sure, to the satisfaction of every fair minded man in this House that the western provinces are entitled to their natural resources, and if any adjustment has to be made it can very easily be taken up after that policy has been put into effect. But as the hon. member for Marquette has stated, there will be no satisfaction amongst the people of the West until this question is settled, and settled right. They look to the Government to settle it now once and for all, and then adjust these other matters between the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), I rise not to debate the whole question, but merely to emphasize two or three points in respect to it. All parties now agree that these natural resources should be returned to the prairie provinces, but some of them make conditions as to that return. That is not a satisfactory situation so far as the prairie provinces are concerned. They base their claim to these resources primarily upon the fact that, treated as they now are, they are regarded as the illegitimate children of Confederation. In a sense that is true. The Manitoba Act of this House which created the province of Manitoba was beyond the Dominion's powers. It was by that Act in the first place that these lands were reserved for the purposes of the Dominion. That legislation was recognized to be ineffectual, and the Imperial Act of 1871 was passed for its legalization and confirmation. It was in the second section of the Imperial Act that the Dominion was first given the power out of its great Rupert's Land domain to create new provinces.
Now, that Act of 1871 was in terms a confirmation of the Manitoba Act for all purposes whatsoever. I have said already that the Federal Act had reserved these lands. But, Sir, the point in the matter is this. Primarily the British North America Act recognized but one species of province -a province severeign within its own limits. The Dominion had certain powers allotted to it, but it was a landless Dom- . inion. Consequently, if a province of the status contemplated by the British North America Act was created-and there was no right to create any other kind-then that province must have its lands. But in the same Act that created the province those lands were withheld from it illegally..

When the confirming Act was passed the situation was peculiar. The province of Manitoba was born in the shame of insurrection, land the fear at that time was that the engagements of the Imperial and Dominion Governments with the Hudson's Bay Company would not be implemented by a legislative assembly elected in Manitoba, where at that time there was bitter feeling againt the Company, which was thought to have betrayed the settlers of Manitoba. So for that temporary purpose the Dominion retained those lands; but what was intended as a temporary retention has developed into the fifty years usurpation which we are now discussing.
If this Act of 1871 is analysed a dilemma is presented. Either it created a province of the description which the British North America Act contemplated, in which case the province has all the powers incident to its status together with the possession of its lands; or else it must hang upon the other horn of the dilemma, that the lands were properly withdrawn from the province. Then what kind of >a province was created? There is legal opinion of respectable authority which claims that if this question were brought before the Privy Council necessarily it would hold to the first of those two positions, that is, that the only province which could be created was a province endowed with all the powers which the British North America Act first proposed; and that the other position-which, it is true, was recognized by the Imperial Parliament, but for a merely temporary purpose because to do otherwise at that time would have been to discredit the Dominion Government in the case of an insurrection-was unconstitutionally enacted, and therefore null and void. That would perhaps place this matter in the position which the Prairie Provinces ask as a basis for any negotiation.
There is another question which I think should be dealt with at some length. It is this. There has been settlement after settlement apparently of the claims which the western provinces had. The first one came about, I believe, in 1883 or thereabouts. Up to that time we had received . in Manitoba nothing in lieu of these lands. Look how the question was then presented to us. We were getting per capita grant up to that time. Then we were offered a little less than $27,000 more provided we would do away with one branch of our legislature. See how one evil step was leading on to another. The Dominion was determining the form of the constitution of the province, something which it had no

right to do, and which to-day if attempted in any of our provinces would bring about a very strained feeling.
After that we made settlement after settlement. But what was our position in all these matters? Practically that of an heir or a beneficiary whose trustee was unfaithful. There have not been bestowed upon us the powers, the rights, the authority, the dominion which belong to our conditions as a province. Indeed, the grants made have been referred to as probably suitable for the keeping up of a seaside hotel, but not such as are requisite to the keeping up of a state, an authority, the administration of a province. Again and again we had to come back here and ask for a portion of our domain or something in lieu of our domain in order that we might carry on.
Now, it may be argued that we are in the position of an heir who has come of age, has condoned the past and made settlement in regard to it. But we have never arrived at our majority, and we cannot do so until we have control of these resources. Not until that time comes shall we be free from pressure. Not until then shall we be free agents to deal with this matter. Oujr necessities have been such, not having the control of the resources to use as required in the development of our provinces, that we have been obliged to accept what was offered. I think Sir Wilfrid Laurier said when the Saskatchewan and Alberta Bills went through that $2,000,000 would be the maximum amount which would be derived yearly from the grants that were then made and the provisions for increasing the grants as population increased. Would the great province of Ontario, the natural resources of which, I venture to say, cannot compare with those of Alberta, be content to take $2,000,000 a year in lieu of her natural resources? She would not think of doing it; she could not be persuaded to consider it for a moment. But such are the terms imposed upon Alberta, because that province is not yet in a position to deal with the matter as equal with equal.
It makes one think of the old Bible story of Joseph and his brethren; when they had sold him into slavery they wanted to divide his coat of many colours among them. That is our position in respect to the claims made by Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for a portion of the natural resources which belong to us. If these other provinces want to be on an equal footing with us, let them surrender their natural resources to the Dominion; that would be an interesting proposal to submit to them. That,

however, is what they ask us to submit to now. Put the shoe on the other foot, and it will very quickly be found that no such arrangement would appeal to them; yet they ask us to accept that position.
Now, finally-for 1 think I have made the two points I wanted to make-let me say that no question is settled until it is settled right. Already in the West such words as " gross " and " villainous " are applied to the deprivation of these provinces of their natural resources. We cannot have within a great state or confederation provinces of different status. It is impracticable; it is fraught with danger. Now is the time to get to a settlement of this vital question within our body politic. I have been a resident of Manitoba for forty years, and during that time there has never been a year when Manitoba has not had a grievance against the Dominion Government. Is that a healthy state of affairs? Is that a healthy condition between a province and a Dominion which is interested in all our affairs? Now, it will never be settled as I say, until it is settled upon right principles.
I cannot think that the other provinces have any right at this stage to intervene. The question is strictly between the Prairie Provinces individually and the Dominion Government. I grant that out of the settlement there may arise certain injustices, but look at what we are getting to-day. We are getting less than $800,000 a year in lieu of these lands in Manitoba. Over 18,000,000 acres of our lands have been disposed of by the Dominion for the purposes of the Dominion. That is less than five per cent upon a valuation of one dollar per acre. Does any man believe that they were worth but one dollar per acre, or that we should ever have disposed of them for any such sum as that? That is the character of the settlement; on the other hand we are told that the Dominion has spent somewhere around $86,000,000 upon the administration of these natural resources and has received only some $44,000,000, leaving $42,000,000 as an adverse balance. That is not taking account, I am free to say, of lands which have been given away for railway purposes- 100,000,000 acres of land in the western provinces have been set aside for the promotion of railways. The lands for purposes of that character were parted with in vast areas. These accountings may have to be settled, as has been suggested, by the Exchequer Court or some other impartial tribunal. There is but one way to
settle this question, and that is to recognize that the western provinces must have the same status as the others; that their resources must be restored to them. Once we accept that principle; once we realize that nothing must prevent that, then we can go into the accounting.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the House very long in the few remarks which I shall make on this very important matter; but I wish to emphasize a few points.
The western provinces believe that the settlement of this question is a matter between the provinces and the Dominion and that the other provinces should not interfere in that settlement. It has been suggested that the western provinces wish to receive the resources so as to swell their provincial treasury. Now I am going to take the liberty of quoting from the budget speech of Hon. Charles A. Dunning, Provincial Treasurer of Saskatchewan, under date November 23rd, 1920, to show that that province at least is not looking for a very much greater revenue through the handling of its natural resources.
This legislature and the people of the province have not been working to have the control of the natural resources of the province transferred to them each year for the past ten years without having in their minds very definite reasons why, in their judgment, the province should secure this control. There is an idea, commonly held in some parts of Canada, that our motive is a financial one. That is to say, that we want to get control of the resources for the purpose of making money out of them.
It cannot he too clearly stated that this is not our motive. Indeed, from the information in our possession relating to the resources and their administration we would he very foolish if we laboured under the misapprehension that it is possible for us to receive any considerable amount of revenue -in excess of what we would be compelled to expend in their development. The best proof that we are not actuated by money consideration is to be found in the records of the Dominion administration of the resources of Western Canada. At the last interprovincial conference at -which I was present as one of those representing the province, the Honourable Arthur Meighen, at that time Minister of the Interior, brought down a lot of figures in order to give the conference information as to the financial position relating to the administration of natural resources by the federal government, and I need only quote from one of the statements to indicate to the House that the Dominion Government, up -to that date, so far from making money out of their handling of our resources had actually lost money.
One of the statements referred to is a statement of expenditure and revenue in connection with Dominion lands in Manitoba, iSaskatche-wan, Alberta and British Columbia from July 1, 1872, to September 30, 1918, for the whole period of Dominion administration of these lands. During that time the expenditure by the Dominion properly chargeable to the adminis-

tration of them, amounted to $86,441,807.60 and the net revenue received, from all these lands was $46,914,171. Up to that time the Dominion's revenue from these resources was less by over thirty-nine and a half millions than their expenditure. Necessarily this is a cash statement. Necessarily, too, there are outstanding amounts in connection with these resources due the Dominion. For instance: payments on pre-emptions. I have no statement as to what those outstanding amounts are but I have no doubt they could not nearly make up this deficiency.
The point is important, Mr. Speaker, that the Dominion has not made money by the administration of our resources and I therefore say that we could not hope to very considerably augment the revenues of the province by getting control of our natural resources. We may, by adopting a different policy, secure greater revenues than the Dominion authorities have, so that the money consideration is not, and never has been, the reason for our demands for control of our natural resources.
The most important reason, to myself at any rate, is that after years of Dominion handling of our resources in Saskatchewan there is practically no industrial development of them. Succeeding federal governments have administered our resources and practically the only industry that has been developed as a result of Dominion administration is agriculture-the top six inches of the soil as some one has called it Useful work, of course, has been done in connection with our land resources, but I submit that the people of our province are vitally interested in the development of their resources other than lands.
The first point that I wish to make is that there is a well-estaiblished British rule in connection with this vital and important question. I quote now from the Manitoba Free Press, which says:
The question put plainly is-Are the western provinces full partners in confederation or are they merely colonies over whom the other provinces exercise a feudal suzerainty which gives them a right to enter upon their possessions and take toll of them.
The case for the provinces rests broadly upon the well-established British principle that the people of a self-governing community have the sole right to the beneficial interest in the public domain. If the principles upon which the Dominion Government has insisted in the case of Manitoba had been applied by Great Britain, the public domain of Canada, Australia and all the British dependencies would be the property of the British Crown and would be administered for the benefit of the treasury of the United Kingdom.	It was
the judgment of Sir Robert Borden, a sound constitutional lawyer, that the arguments by which the Dominion seeks to retain control of the public domain in the West "would have justified the' retention by the Imperial Government up to the present time of every acre of Crown lands in Canada." Hansard, 1905.
I contend that, quoting from the Manitoba Free Press, I have shown that there is a well-established principle under British rule that the lands of a province belong to

the people living in that province. The Manitoba Free Press continues:
In 1864 the Hudson Bay Company expressed a willingness to have the Red river district formed into a Crown colony, provided the company could retain a considerable proprietary control of the lands. The Colonial Office declined the proposal. "The whole progress of the colony," said the Colonial Office, "depends on the liberal and prudent disposal of the land. It is clear that colonists of the Anglo-Saxon race look upon the land revenue as legtiknately belonging to the community." If the Red river settlement had become a Crown colony under Downing street, which was the practical alternative to union with Canada, there would have been no question about the ownership of these lands ; they would have become the property of the community. By joining the Canadian Confederation, Manitoba earned the reward of being robbed of her public lands.
But we shall be told with damnable iteration that these rules do not apply because the Dominion Government bought this country from the Hudson Bay Company and, therefore, owns the lands and the minerals and the forests and the water powers and the fisheries. Most of the people who make these assertions are densely ignorant of the circumstances attending the transfer of Western Canada to the Dominion. They appear to think that Canada entered into direct negotiations with the Hudson Bay Company, bought out its interests for cash and took over the country. Western Canada did not thus pass direct from the company to Canada. The Imperial Government dealt with the company; and after taking over the territory it was transferred to Canada by Imperial Order in Council. In December, 1869, the Dominion Government in a communication to the Colonial Office insisted that this procedure be followed "On surrender by company to Queen," said the cablegram, "the government of the company ceases. The responsibility of administration of affairs will then rest upon the Imperial Government. Canada cannot accept transfer unless quiet possession is given." When the Canadian Government sent this notification to the Imperial Government it had already agreed to pay £300,000 compensation to the Hudson Bay Company for relinquishing of its claim to an interest in the lands. Despite this engagement it desired the country to pass for a period under Imperial control; and this was the procedure followed. The surrender to the Crown by the company was signed on Nevember 19, 1869 ; the money was paid on May 11, 1870 ; on June 22, 1870, the Imperial Government accepted the surrender; and on July 15, 1870, the country was transferred by the Imperial Government. Thus subsequent to the payment of the money Western Canada was for nearly a month a part of the Imperial system under the direct authority of Downing street and subject to the principle that the public lands of a community are under the control of the people of that district. When the territory passed to Canada >
on July 15, did the people lose the rights which they were certainly in possession of during the period of Imperial occupation?
It may be urged that this is a legal and technical argument. Very well; let us consider it on the basis of moral rights. The Hudson Bay Company insisted upon dealing with the British Government in reaching an agreement upon which it would give possession on payment of certain sums in compensa-

tion ; and the Bill authorizing the negotiations if passed in its original form, would have mad£>
the payment of the compensation a charge on the Imperial treasury. The Bill passed the House of 'Lords in this form, but in its passage through the House of Commons a further provision was made that no charge against the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom should lie as the result of these negotiations. Accordingly, Canada had to agree to put up the money or see the negotiations fail. Now, if the United Kingdom had paid the £300,000, would the British Government have claimed the right to own and administer the public domain in Western Canada to this day? In 18*67 the British Government bought out the rights of the Hudson Bay Company in Vancouver Island, but neither the control of the land nor the beneficial interest therein was retained by the Imperial Government. They were vested in the province of British Columbia, and when, subsequent to the entrance of Manitoba into Confederation, British Columbia was admitted, no question of its right to its natural resources was raised. If the British Government had settled with the Hudson Bay Company there would have equally been no question of the disposition of the lands of Western Canada. But the Canadian Government, in contempt of the sound British principle of which they had themselves been the beneficiary, usurped in 1870 the right of Manitoba to control her domain and has ever since retained possession of the lands then seized.
I have quoted from these western papers, and I could quote from others, the Saskatoon Star, for instance, but it is not necessary, in order that the House may understand that it is the wish of practically all the people of the western provinces that their natural resources be handed over forthwith. I also wish to state that they support the stand taken by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in his addresses last winter through the western provinces, to the effect that the natural resources should be handed over forthwith to the provinces, and that if the other provinces of the Dominion have any claims, those claims should be settled in the court of law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The subject of the restoration
of the natural resources of the western provinces to those provinces has been a subject of political debate in Canada for many years. It is a topic upon which it is one of the easiest tasks in the world to make a speech, and as to the solution of which it is one of the most difficult tasks to make any substantial progress. The difficulty is that the resources were withheld at the time of the constitution of the provinces. In the case of Manitoba that took place in the early 70's. The reason given for the withholding of the resources and the substitution in their place of a cash subsidy,
161J	'
was that it was essential at that time that the lands and other resources should be under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, as otherwise it would be in the power of the provinces to place, practical obstacles in the way of immigration. Had the lands been transferred the key, as it were, to immigration and the settlement of the West would have been transferred largely to the province itself. Whatever may have been the foundation of that claim in 1871, it does not, and never did, seem to me that it had very much force in the year 1905.
I am not saying that other claims were not advanced. Other reasons were given particularly in 1905, and constituted the main reasons for the withholding of the resources then. I did not agree with those reasons. I have never given much weight to the contention that has been refuted by, I think, every speaker who has preceded me in this debate, that there was some special charge against the western country because the Hudson Bay lands or charter were acquired by the Dominion. Nor have I given any weight at all to the argument many times presented, and also refuted by all my predecessors in this debate, that there has been, because the West was later opened up than the East, some special debt owing by Western Canada to Eastern Canada, a debt that must be recouped out of the resources of the West. I am not able to understand how such contentions can be seriously advanced. I do not think there is any special obligation of the West to the East, or of the East to the West. But the resources were withheld. An arrangement was come to between the representatives here of those provinces at that time, and the government of the day in Ottawa, that they should be withheld.

What does the right
hon. gentleman refer to by "those provinces"? Who were these men representatives of?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The representatives of the districts that became the provinces. My recollection is that the Hon. Walter Scott was one; I think the Hon. Frank Oliver was another; I could name several more. I mean the representatives of the territory afterwards embraced in the provinces.
They had no official standing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They had as members for the district, and they acquiesced in the settlement. They did not represent the provinces as provinces, because the pro-

vinces were not then created, hut no doubt in the arrangement that was arrived at they exercised their voice. It is inconceivable that they did not, and it is a matter of history that .they acquiesced therein, and went out into those newly created provinces and recommended the settlement arrived at as fair to the districts and fair to the provinces as such, and the appeals they made on that ground were accepted as sound by the people of the provinces, and the people of the provinces, basing their action largely on those appeals, returned governments to power in sympathy with the settlement. That does not say that it was in consonance with British practice to withhold lands or other resources from provinces when created, but it does say that the lands and other resources were withheld, and it does say that the governments taking office in provinces so created, from which the lands and resources were withheld, and the people of those provinces, as far as they could speak on the subject in an election succeeding, acquiesced in the arrangements so made, and to that extent became parties thereto. It argues also that it does not lie very strongly in the mouth of those who at that time approved the step that was taken, a step far more easily avoided than retraced, to come now and make a very strong plea that a grave injustice at the time was perpetrated, an injustice which a succeeding government must take the responsibility of undoing. Anyway, the fact is that the arrangement was made. The resources were witheld, and subsidy in lieu of lands was given, given to those provinces1 and to those alone. Manitoba contended for many years that her subsidy in lieu of lands was much less than the others, and was able to effect in 1912 a settlement whereby she was placed on the same basis as the later sister in confederation, receiving the arrears and an extension	of	boundaries	commensurate with theirs. So they all came on the same footing in 1912. It is contended by speakers who have preceded me-and I cannot help but note a unanimous silence on the part of hon. gentlemen directly opposite-that the other provinces, as provinces, have no concern in this matter; that as the western provinces for some years back, as now, have demanded the return of their resources, it is a subject to be settled wholly between the Federal Government and the governments of those provinces. There is this to be said on the other side: that inasmuch as the subsidy in lieu of lands was given 
and has been paid throughout these years and is still current, and as subsidies are matters that affect all the provinces, and as a special subsidy given to one immediately becomes the right of the others, unless that one can be differentiated, there in that fact lies the interest of the other province ;. If Manitoba were coming and saying: "Give us our lands and our resources and keep your subsidy," then there would be some force in the statement of hon. gentlemen that this is a question beween the Federal Government and the governments of the western provinces; there would be considerable force in that suggestion, in the minds of those who are in sympathy with the contention that there is no special charge leviable against the western prairies in favour of the east, and that means, that it would have very considerable force, with me.
Is not Manitoba entitled to some compensation for the resources that have already been alienated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will come to that; I would never leave lout so important a factor of the problem. But on that ground the other provinces come, not just upon invitation; they do not particularly need invitation, }VIr. Speaker. I have had sufficient to do with the governments of the other provinces of Canada, and particularly the governments of the Maritime Provinces, to know that they do not need special inducements held out to come and make claims when there is anything in the way of subsidies being adjusted.
Were they not given a specific invitation to come in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have been given an invitation to all provincial conferences. Other subjects have been taken up at provincial conferences, and the provinces are all entitled to be present at every provincial conference. We have had a conference on this special subject alone within the last few months, during the time the present Government has been in office, and to that they were not given any special invitation because it was not in any way an interprovincial conference. I have said that they have come in, and because the question of subsidies was involved they have claimed that they have an interest and a right to be consulted when there is any question of the readjustment of subsidies; and to that claim, it seems to me, it was pretty hard to give a negative answer.

Who indeed says a negative answer should be given to the claim that they have a right to be heard? Hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon have said so; but the party whom they were charging with great neglect of duty and abandonment of promises have never taken that ground. The late Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), when in opposition, and ever since, in relation to the question of returning the resources, has always stated that fair terms had first to be arranged. Now, I know that no leader of a party can escape from a promise merely because it declared that there had to be fair terms. If fair terms are afterwards presented, terms which he cannot argue are manifestly unfair, and he refuses them, he is guilty of conduct not consistent with the promise on which he obtained office. But is that the case? I will come to that in a moment. Hon. gentlemen directly opposite-and I am not making an attack on them now, because so far, in this debate, they have preserved a silence which I could not help appreciating-have taken the ground, officially, that the other provinces have a concern and an interest in this matter. Not only have they taken that ground, but members of the governments of the three provinces affected have taken it and, indeed, have led in the movement that culminated in the official and formal recognition by hon. gentlemen opposite of the interest of the other provinces in the matter. At the Liberal convention held in August, 1919, a particular resolution, appearing among an almost interminable number of resolutions, and dealing with this question, was moved by the Prime Minister of Alberta, seconded by the Prime Minister of Saskatchewan, and acquiesced in, as the report says, unanimously, which, 1 presume, means acquiesced in by the Prime Minister of Manitoba. I did not know myself that Hon. Mr. Norris was at the convention as I had no record of the proceedings; but I heard in the debate on the Address the claim made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), I think it was, that the Prime Minister of Manitoba was in the fold at that convention. Consequently this resolution can be said to have been acquiesced in by the heads of all the governments of the three western provinces. The resolution reads:
Resolved, that the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted the ownership and control of the natural resources within their respective boundaries on terms that are fair and equitable with reference to all the other provinces of the Dominion.
So that the heads of the governments of these provinces, who hon. gentlemen who have spoken say must alone be satisfied- they say it is a question that must be settled between us and them-have themselves gone officially on record-I do not care whether you describe it as officially or otherwise-as recognizing the interests of the other provinces in the matter; and no doubt they would base the recognition on the claim that subsidies must be affected in some way or other when the resources are returned. That is the position of the matter.	[DOT]
Now, the question arises: Has this Government been in a position, is it in a position to-day, to return those resources upon fair terms? Let us assume for the moment that this resolution is wrong; that those of us are wrong who say that it is better in this matter that the other provinces should be consulted and that we should endeavour, if we can, to come to an arrangement satisfactory to all; let us assume that we are wrong in that respect and that only the Dominion and the governments of the three provinces are concerned. Now, have the governments of the three provinces manifested a desire to settle this matter upon terms that any of us in this House could consider as fair? Let me ask hon. gentlemen opposite and on this side whether any proposal which those governments have so far put forward has been such that any Government of Canada could grant the resources on the terms suggested? What are the proposals they have put forward? Originally, they made this proposal, which is the only definite one I have heard so far: "We will accept the return of the natural resources provided you permit us to retain entirely the subsidy in lieu of lands that was given us for those resources. That was the position they took before at least one of the Provincial Conferences, a position which I understand they maintained until very lately. Let us consider that. Hon. gentlemen will have the right to say in this debate whether it is the duty of the Government of the day to return those resources and at the same time to continue the payment of the extra subsidy, and whether they will undertake to support a Government that will take that step.
What next? In a recent communication, which I understand was laid on the table of the Manitoba House the Prime Minister of that province has taken another position and has withdrawn even from that offer. Now what, reduced to

plain English, is the position he takes? He says: " We cannot any longer stand hy the proposal we made that you give us the natural resources the same as the other provinces and keep on ppying us the extra subsidy-the whole of it-as well. We withdraw that because you did not accept it, and we ask you to do this: We ask you to declare that the Dominion has been the trustee of those [DOT] resources, notwithstanding the Acts of 1905 establishing the province. We ask you to declare that the Dominion has been the trustee of those . resources and is accountable as trustee to the provinces for the disposition of all those resources from that day to this." Not only does he say that but he also says: You must account in a fiduciary capacity and if you have alienated-as he described it-any of the lands or other resources for less than the value of those lands, or resources, you must, in the accounting, make good to us what the lands were worth-[DOT] what might have been obtained for them in the open market. That is to say: If the Dominion did-as it did in 1905, yes and long before-have a homesteading policy and gave free homesteads to those who wanted to go into that prairie country, to enter there and become pioneers and settlers-if the Dominion adopted that policy and gave free homesteads and thereby contributed to the building up ,of those provinces-you must now give an account to the Government of those provinces for what you could have sold that land for if you had not adopted any homesteading policy at all.
That is the proposal that is now advanced officially by the Government of Manitoba, and that is the only other proposal that we have had except the one that I mentioned first-that the entire subsidy be retained and that the lands be given back as well. Not only shbuld we accoun: for the value of the homesteads granted- and remember the homesteading policy was adopted in order to build up the provinces, in order to build up the country primarily; first the West where the homesteads were and ultimately the whole Dominion-but it is seriously suggested that the Dominion now should account for what it might have received if it had retarded western development by a system of sale instead of a system of homesteading. The same requirement he seeks to apply not only as regards homesteading but to the administration of the other resources of the West as well.
But there is this other objection to what is advanced in the latest proposal: Is it

even a possible method of solution? It cannot be assumed that you can place the Dominion Government down at a desk as it were and have it mark on one side the figures representing the moneys it has received in respect of western lands, and have it tabulate on the other side the moneys that it has disbursed because of the retention of western lands. Such a tabulation in either case is impossible. The fact is that the lands were retained, the resources were retained, and the public policy has adjusted itself to those facts ever since; and in practically every phase of public policy that relates to Western Canada account has been taken of the fact that the lands and resources were so retained. Is it to be said that the actual moneys disbursed because of the retention of the land and resources can be with any certainty ascertained? Is it to be said that the moneys we have spent in the administration of homesteads, the administration of grazing lands, the administration of western fisheries in the administration of irrigation, the administration of forest and water-powers can be divided and the portion attributable to the federal ownership of those resources arrived at? Why that could not be said at all. What about the money spent in respect of immigration? Can anybody say there would have been anything like the money spent for immigration in this country if it had not been for the fact that the western lands and resources were retained under Federal control? Can anyone venture to say how much of the moneys disbursed for immigration was not attributable to the fact that the lands were federally retained and how much was not attributable to that fact? He who would attempt the task of apportioning the money spent on immigration alone, or between one class and the other, would be attempting, I venture to submit, an utterly impossible task. And you can pass from immigration to other subjects- subjects in respect of drainage, in respect of water-power, in respect of irrigation, in respect of railways.
In all these matters the Dominion, in adopting the policy it pursued had regard to the fact that these resources were under federal responsibility, and that we have had control:	The expenditure of the Dominion would have been different had the lands originally been made the property of the provinces and not the property of the Dominion. It is not a hard matter to scramble an egg but it is a very hard matter to unscramble it. It was not a hard matter to retain the resources, but

once you have retained them for fifteen to twenty years and adjusted every phase of public policy to the fact that there was that retention, then it becomes a matter of very great complexity. Indeed it becomes a matter in the solution of which you meet with obstacles at every step and to such an extent that no half-dozen men can agree on any stage. It becomes a matter with respect to which it is impossible to arrive at anything like an accounting on a trustee basis at all. Consequently I have argued-and I have argued very recently with the prime ministers of these provinces -that we do not get any further by trying to establish and admit the principle that the lands originally should have been transferred. You do not get any further by setting up that trustee principle-as "a great white flame" if we only keep our eye on it will settle this matter on the eternal basis of right-you do not get any further by that method. You may get further by one way, and one way only, by presenting some concrete proposal in figures that will appeal to a fair-minded man as a square, bald, rough but honourable solution.

In 1911 Sir
Robert Borden the prospective premier, promised us that if he was returned to power he would give to the western provinces their natural resources. Have the difficulties of doing that multiplied very much since then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Was the Government,
which the hon. gentleman supported, the Government in power at that time, ready to take those resources unless it got the subsidies as well? Sir Robert Borden did not say he would give the provinces the subsidies as well as the resources; and the provinces have never agreed to take the resources unless they keep the subsidies as well. They have indicated a desire to take the resources and the subsidies too, and now one has abandoned even that: that is the situation we are in to-day. The difficulties have multiplied jsince 1905-* undoubtedly as difficulties always do-and they will not be any less as the years go by. I for one would very much like to see a spirit of greater reasonableness enter into the discussion of this question. It is an easy matter to make speeches, but as long as the heads of government take their stand definitely and finally where they have taken it, then-whether the other provinces have a right to he heard or not- we are not making very much progress
towards getting to an end of the question. Now something may be done to help by a study of all the different phases of legislation, by a study of the moneys directly received and the moneys directly and indirectly expended, Remember they are far greater than the figures indicated by the hon. member for Nelson-that is the moneys disbursed, There may be something done in the way of throwing light on what would be a fair apportionment of subsidy received in lieu of lands. I would like indeed if we could be met in a spirit of conciliation in an effort to get at some half way place where we could meet and settle this matter once for all, but I must say that I have not been very much encouraged by the attitude of those who on the one hand say, "We must have our resources back, and we must have the money as well;" and who later retract that and say, "No, we will take the resources on one basis only, that you account to us for everything you have done with these lands, and if you have not got all the money in hand that you should have derived from them we will make you account to us for what you might have obtained." There is not very much encouragement when you are met in that spirit. Therefore it seems to me that the House will not agree with any resolution which implies that this Government has been in any way negligent in endeavouring to seek a solution of this question.
I come from Western Canada myself, and I know that there is a feeling more or less general that the Prairie Provinces have a just grievance in this regard, that they are not on a parity with the other provinces as regards their autonomy. On that account I would especially like to see this question settled. I am not in hopes that we will ever arrive at a time when the provinces of the West feel that they have no grievance at all in respect to federal affairs. My experience is such that I am afraid it will be a long time before we reach the stage when every province will concede that it has no grievance in respedt to federal affairs. This is such an extensive country, and some of our provinces are so far from the others, that each particular province feels that all its sisters have been treated well and it has been treated very ill. That is the case in the West as well as in other parts of the Dominion.
I have always felt that the western provinces have a right to the same autonomous jurisdiction as the other provinces. It would be well for the whole Confedera-

tion if the premiers of these provinces would meet the Federal Government and strive towards some fair compromise which would appeal to the other provinces and to their representatives here as a sensible basis fair to all, and one that all or most of us could join to support.

Does not my right hon.
friend think it possible to settle the question of what subsidies shall be paid to the western provinces in lieu of the lands or resources by reference to the courts or by arbitration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You might settle it
by arbitration, but I do not think that outsiders coming in to arbitrate could do as well as the heads of the governments themselves. You could not settle it in the courts, because there is no principle to go on. I would be only too glad if this was a question of law, then it could easily be relegated to the courts and there decided -a solution devoutly to be wished.

Why not send it to the
Exchequer Court?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Exchequer Court
is a court of law, and it would have to decide the question on principles- of law. If it were such a question it would not be very long troubling the Government; that is where it would be; but it is not such a question. Nor does it seem to me that we could get very far by arbitration.
