You would have to arrive at mutual concessions, and you would have to have some principles which the Board of Arbitration could follow to decide what portion of any special class of expenditure was attributable to the fact that the Dominion retained the resources; and to get an accounting on anything like a fiduciary basis seems to me a task beyond the capacity of the human mind. At best it can only be got at in a rough way, and can never be reached until both sides approach the matter in a fair and conciliatory spirit.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was very quick to remark that there had been what appeared to him unanimous silence from the official Opposition. I would direct his attention to the fact that some eight or nine speeches were made from this side of the House without a single hon. member on the Government side rising to make a reply or response of any kind. If the official Opposition delayed to take part in this debate, it was not with any intention of evading a statement of its position. We

were naturally expecting that with the large following which the Government has on its side some one would rise to state the position of hon. gentlemen opposite. The truth, of course, is that this is a question that primarily affects the West, and the western representatives who are sitting on this side of the House took advantage of the earliest opportunity to rise and state their position. What, I think, will strike the country as something more than a coincidence is the circumstance that while hon. gentlemen opposite have in their ranks a number of representatives of western constituencies, not one of those representatives has risen to say a single word in support of this resolution.
Let me say at once that so far as the Liberal Opposition is concerned, we are heartily in accord with the resolution, which has been moved and which is in the following terms:
That, in the opinion of this House, the transfer by the Dominion to the Western Provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta of their natural resources should not be longer
delayed.
There are two important statements in that resolution. First of all there is the statement of principle, that these resources should be transferred to the western provinces; with that principle we are in entire accord. Then there is the statement that the resources should be transferred without delay. This, I think, must appear obviously desirable when we realize that the longer this question is left in the open the longer will it be before the western provinces will feel that they have had that mead of justice from the Dominion to which they are entitled.
Therefore our position, as stated by my right hon. friend, is as set out in the resolution passed by the Liberal convention held in this city in August of 1919. It is as follows:
That the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted the ownership and control of the natural resources within their respective boundaries on terms that are fair and equitable with reference to all the other provinces of the Dominion.
Some exception has been taken to the words, "fair and equitable with reference to all the other provinces of the Dominion." So far as those words are capable of any interpretation other than what appears on their face, they can mean only "on terms that are just." The contention of some of the western provinces that just terms are to be arrived at in one way rather than another is a perfectly proper

contention. I do not wish at the moment to debate the question as to what are fair and equitable terms; but this I do say, that if you reverse the statement and assume that any other than fair and equitable terms are to be conceded, you get a resolution that I am sure even my western friends would not support. It would then read:
That the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted the ownership and control of the natural resources within their respective boundaries, on terms that are unfair and inequitable with reference to all the other provinces of the Dominion.
Do my western friends want that? I am sure that no hon. gentleman who has spoken to-night would say that he would like to see the western provinces get a transfer of their natural resources on terms that were inequitable or unfair to the other provinces of the Dominion. Unless they are prepared to support that position, it seems to me they ought to be prepared, in justice to the Dominion as a whole to take the very reasonable view which has been set forth and agree to the transfer of these resources on terms that are equitable and fair.
At this hour of the night, especially after the matter has been gone into so fully, I do not think it is necessary to argue at any length the different points that arise for consideration. But this I would say:	there is a responsibility upon the
Government, if it asserts a particular policy, to see that that policy is carried out. I am sure that the country will view with a sense of amazement and disappointment the remarks of my right hon. friend to-night, which imply that instead of being anxious to effect an immediate settlement of this question the Government is looking rather to a way of avoiding a settlement altogether. My right hon. friend has repeatedly said "if we could get this or that proposal put up to us and we regarded it as fair, we might be prepared to accept it." I think, Mr. Speaker, that is looking at the matter entirely from the wrong point of view. It is not for the provinces to come along and make a policy for the Government; it is for the Government to have a policy and to see that it is carried out. That is the position which we on this side at least are prepared to take. We have a policy and we are prepared to stand by it; we are prepared to see, if entrusted with the duty of administering the affairs of this country, that our policy is carried out.	I

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (West Calgary) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) took occasion to suggest that he was greatly surprised that no member for Western Canada on the Government side had spoken in support of this resolution, but I did not see the necessity of supporting the resolution when every hon. gentleman who had spoken had done so. While the good work was going on I thought it might be wise that I should retain my seat and give the hon. leader of the Opposition an opportunity to express his views.
It is true that the question of the transfer to the western provinces of their natural resources is a question of very great importance, one that has engaged the attention of the western people ever since 1905. But as the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) has pointed out, the responsibility for the dilemma in which we now find ourselves is in no sense attributable to any policy which was advocated by Sir Robert Borden or carried out by the Government of which he was leader nor to the policy of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) or his Government. In 1905, if any public question was ever put fairly and squarely before the people, it was certainly the question of the Autonomy Bills affecting Alberta and Saskatchewan, and if any party ever stood loyally behind a government in the deprivation of the people of that to which they were justly entitled, it was the Liberal party-especially its western supporter^-led by 'Sir Wilfrid Laurier when his government deliberately robbed the people of the western country of those resources to which they were entitled in the creation of the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
When the matter was taken up by the Laurier Government representatives came from the Northwest Territories to advocate our cause. Those who came from the Northwest Territories and who were associated with the legislative assembly and government of the Territories were fully imbued with the idea that when the new western provinces were created their natural resources would be given to them and that they would have complete autonomy so far as their civil, religious, educational and property rights were concerned. But when the Government of the day of which the hon. leader of the Opposition was at one time a member, had disposed of the matter, those gentlemen who had been sent here to procure complete autonomy at any cost, returned to Western

Canada, not with the natural resources, not with a general public school system for the provinces, but they returned, one gentleman as lieutenant governor of Alberta, another as the Premier of Saskatchewan, and another with a seat in the Senate, while the retainers at home secured suitable rewards. Only one, Sir Frederick Haultain, at that time leader of the Government in the Legislature of the Northwest Territories, remained loyal to the interests of Western Canada. The present condition, therefore, is due wholly and solely to the fact that the people of Western Canada were betrayed by the men who came down here to settle the terms of the Autonomy Bills creating those two provinces.
As to the position taken by Sir Robert Borden in Western Canada, it has been suggested by those opposed to him-and the statement has been made on every platform and in every election-that when Sir Robert Borden toured Western Canada during the election campaign of 1911 he said that if he were returned to power the natural resources of Western Canada would be transferred to the respective provinces concerned. There seems to be some dispute as to the exact words that he used. But assuming for the purpose of argument that he made a definite promise in that regard, what was the attitude of the people of Western Canada? What was the attitude of the Liberal party? What was the attitude of the Liberal legislatures of Alberta and Saskatchewan? My own province was toured from one end to the other by all Liberal senators, by all Liberal members of the House of Commons, by all Liberal members of the Legislature of Alberta, and all members of the Provincial Cabinet, who impressed the people of that province with the argument that they had made the best possible arrangement, whereby they received cash subsidies in lieu of lands and that they would make a mistake if they returned Robert Borden to power for the purpose of securing to the western provinces their natural resources. Their argument prevailed; their doctrine was accepted, and every representative from Alberta, with the exception of one was returned to this House because of his opposition to the transfer of the natural resources to the province of Alberta.

Was that the issue in
1911?

That certainly was
the issue. I never attended one session of 
the Legislature of Alberta subsequent to that time when Liberal members of the legislature did not stand up in their places in the House and say that Sir Robert Borden had promised the transfer of the natural resources. If Sir Robert Borden did not make that the issue certainly every Liberal candidate in Alberta and Saskatchewan did so. They urged that we should retain the money subsidies which we were receiving and let the natural resources remain under the control qf the Dominion Government. As a result of that policy; as a result of the conduct of the Laurier Government and Liberal members of the local legislatures, we find ourselves in this hopeless state of chaos to-day.
I will not be as indefinite as the leader of the Opposition is in the matter of a stand on the question of natural resources. [DOT] I am not a convert to the doctrine; I have always taken the view that when these provinces were created they should have had their natural resources. I have supported resolutions in the Alberta Legislature along with my Liberal friends, requesting the Dominion Government to transfer the natural resources to the government of the province of Alberta. I have nothing to apologize for; I have nothing to explain away. The leader of the Opposition stands up to-night and announces a right-about-face policy. He has had a change of heart; he preaches a new gospel; he lays down a new doctrine. He cannot tell us why he departs from the principles advocated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, by Hon. Frank Oliver, Hon. Walter Scott, Hon. Mr. Bulyea, Dr. Rutherford (Premier), Alberta, and others from the West. My stand in this matter has been consistent. As a westerner I am not afraid to say that I believe it is the duty of this Government, if they can possibly do so, to work out some scheme whereby this question of natural resources will be settled. I do, however, not believe it should be the policy of the Government to plunder the public treasury by giving exorbitant cash grants and subsidies to the eastern provinces in order that the western provinces may be given the control of their resources. We have had our public treasury plundered in connection with railway construction in this country, but I do not propose to advocate that that plundering go on in connection with this question. When we can get down to a reasonable basis, when we can get unity in this country, then I say that these natural resources should be handed over to the three western pro-

vinces. The very gentlemen who landed us in the dilemma in which we are at the present time are the people who control the legislatures of the whole of the Dominion of Canada. Every province in Canada, with the exception of Ontario, which has a Farmer government, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, has a Liberal premier, I believe. Those people united on the policy of depriving us of our natural resources. If they have the same heartburnings as the members of the Progressive party have, and as the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggests to this House that he has, cannot they say to the representatives of the great Liberal party:	"Come together in the city of
Ottawa in provincial conference, determine the respective rights of the various provinces, and settle this question? The Liberal party, as a Liberal party, has never had a greater opportunity in this country to settle any great public question than it has to settle the question of our natural resources. It is a matter of deliberation and agreement on the part of those provincial premiers and of the leaders and adherents of the Liberal party. If they had the interest of the whole of Canada, and, in particular, Western Canada, at heart, they could meet together and in a short deliberation, arrive at an agreement which would be acceptable to this House, which would be accepted by this Government, which would settle for all time the question of subsidies for the eastern provinces and the handing over to the western provinces of their natural resources, of which they were deprived by a Liberal administration.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we were listening to a very interesting and fair discussion of the natural resources of the western provinces until the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) came into the debate, and he has imparted an amount of heat and partisanship to it which I deeply regret. I am going to ask him to remember that only a few minutes ago he stated that the people of the western provinces had been betrayed by the Laurier Government, and' that the Laurier Government had robbed the people of the West of their resources.

I beg the hon. member's pardon. That is not my expression. I say that we were betrayed by the people who were sent here from the West to present our interests to the Laurier Government, not by the Laurier Government, and
those people who came here, instead of bringing back the natural resources, took back leaderships, governorships and other offices in connection with public life.

I renew my statement that the hon. member declared that the West had been robbed of its resources by the Laurier Government. I do not argue whether that is true or not; but I will put to my hon. friend a question which will arise in the mind of every western or, indeed, eastern man. All that happened many years ago. We have had ten years now of Conservative Government in one form or another in Canada. If the western provinces were robbed so many years ago, why have the Conservative Government, during the last ten years, not made good the robbery and restored the resources?

I will endeavour to
answer that-because we got in such a hopeless dilemma that we could not.

My hon. friend, and nobody else, is getting into the hopeless dilemma. Even if there had been no pledge to give the western provinces their resources, that should not have needed pledges. If robbery of this character was committed at that time, my hon. friend and his friends have had ten years in which to make good the robbery, to do justice. They have not done justice, and they are here to-day, not attempting to do anything at all. That is the position they occupy. Pledges were given by the former Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). It is not necessary to dwell upon what they were; everybody knows them. What do we find to-day? After all these years, my right hon. friend and his friends are actually saying: "We are not going to do anything to-day." I am amazed at the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) that he is going to oppose the resolution. I did not think it was possible for any one to oppose it. I do not agree with all that my western friends say, but I do agree with the terms of the resolution which simply says:
That, i-n the opinion of this House, the transfer by the Dominion to the western provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, of their natural resources should not be longer delayed.
That is a reasonable proposition, and surely no hon. member can argue that the matter should be longer delayed. Accor' ding to the statement of the Prime Minister, nothing is to be done at all; he gives us no help. With what my right hon. friend said as to the history of the matter,

I largely agree. He correctly described the circumstances under which the resources were withheld from the western provinces. You have to go back to the story of Manitoba from the beginning. It was under the guidance and direction of Sir John A. Macdonald that that province was created. For the reasons stated by the Prime Minister it was held to be wise that the Dominion Government should withhold the control of those resources, because they were believed to be necessary to the Government of the Dominion in the development of a policy of immigration and settlement. It is not necessary to declare that Sir John A. Macdonald was a robber. The policy began in his day and every word that the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Tweedie) says to-day as to the Laurier Government would apply to Sir Jt>hn A. Macdonald, because it was in his day that the policy of withholding the natural resources was adopted. When the Autonomy Bills were passed, for the organization of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, naturally the Government of the day followed the policy laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald and for the same reasons. In that day it was believed that the reason was a good one. The view of Sir John A. Macdonald in the case of Manitoba was considered a sound view and we adopted it in 1905. I say that while it was a good policy in that day, it might not be a good policy to-day. I have perfectly clear views as to what would be a fair solution of the question. My only complaint in regard to the Government is that they are making excuses for doing nothing; they are not pretending to do anything. The true policy of the Government is to settle the matter themselves; to determine upon a policy themselves; to express it in a resolution or in a Bill in this House. If the West will not accept that, the Government will have done their share. The trouble is that the Prime Minister does not indicate a desire to do anything. He is making excuses, talking about a conference of the provinces. I do not see any need of a conference of the provinces. I cannot agree with my western friends who say that the eastern provinces have no interest in this matter. The Eastern provinces have an interest, but I do not think it is an interest in regard to which it is necessary to consult them in any particular way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend mistakes what I said. I did not suggest another conference of the provinces. I

stated that the three provinces that were concerned would not accept any solution now that appeared to me as being fair. I would like the hon. member to say whether he thinks the position they take is fair.

I am rather inclined to think that that position, described by my right hon. friend, is an extreme one. The obligation however rests upon the Government to do something, to make absolutely clear what they are willing to do, and not to make excuses that one or another of the provinces make some claim that the right hon. getleman thinks is extreme. The responsibility rests upon the Government to settle the matter. They should come forward and take the initiative; they should not talk about the necessity of consulting the other provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We cannot force a
settlement on them.

The hon. member can state exactly what it is he is prepared to do. He can lay down the principles upon which he is prepared to settle this matter and make an offer to the western provinces of what he is willing to do. As far as I know, he has never done so. He has availed himself of every excuse for doing nothing and in that respect our western friends have much reason to complain. Speaking for myself, I have no hesitation in saying what my idea is regarding a settlement of this matter. Some of the western men have advanced the view that they were entitled to the subsidies and the lands both. I do not think that is a reasonable position at all. When the constitutions were given to Alberta and Saskatchewan, the resources were withheld and a subsidy was given, in addition to the ordinary subsidy, in lieu of the resources. The policy was acceptable to the authorities of the day. One hon. gentleman to-day says: There was nobody to accept it. The only persons responsible who could deal with the matter at 'the time were those in Parliament, and the general feeling at the time was that the arrangements made were not ungenerous to the new provinces.
I think the general feeling was that the allowance made in lieu of lands and resources was a fair one. I do not remember any opposition to it; I do not remember anybody contending that the arrangement was unreasonable. But if in the progress of time, with the building up of the West, it has become a matter of pride with them to have their natural resources, I would like them to have them, but on fair and

reasonable terms. I do not see that there need be any great difficulty as to what the terms should be. If they want the lands and the subsidies both, I say that is not fair. I entirely endorse the attitude of the Government in saying they will not give them that. But a fair arrangement could be arrived at in one of two ways. You might attempt an accounting, a trusteeship. The right hon. gentleman has said that there are very grave difficulties in the way of that; he may be correct, hut if it were possible I would willingly have a trusteeship,-not in the fiduciary sense he speaks of, whereby this Government would be penalized for giving homesteads for building up the provinces-I would not support that-but I think it would be reasonable to say: Let the Government be treated as trustees from the very beginning. Credit every penny we have received from these resources, and charge as far as may be possible, on the other side, every penny of outlay, including an allowance for general charges which it is difficult to determine. That may be as difficult as my right hon. friend has suggested; it may be impossible, but I would willingly see an effort made to deal with the matter in that way. There is an easier and a simpler way. I do not think it would be an unjust way to say: We will start afresh; you take the resources, and we will keep the money; by-gones will be by-gones. The only sense in which the eastern provinces have anything to do with the matter, is in relation to the subsidy. Some claims have been advanced in some of the provinces in connection with these matters which I do not wish to discuss here. I do not think it is necessary. I think it would be perfectly fair for us to say to the West: We will give you from this moment the resources, and we will stop the subsidy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We would be quite ready to do that, if it could be acceptable.

I think the Government have not hitherto said that. It is not up to the eastern provinces to settle the matter in conference or otherwise. The responsibility is on the Government. They can say to the western provinces: Here is a fair offer; we are willing to enter into an accounting for a trusteeship from the beginning. If that is not possible, we will give you the resources from July 1, and from that day we will pay no more subsidy It would not be reasonable to ask for subsidy and lands both. I am persuaded that on full discussion our friends from
the West will feel that that is not a fair and reasonable proposition.
Would you charge up the western railways against that expenditure?
I would not charge any railway aid against the provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise not to intervene at
any length, in this debate, but just to call attention to the position which we have reached in view of the speech of the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and the speech to which we have just listened by the hon. the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
As I understand it, there is no divergence of opinion as to whether the natural resources should be returned to the provinces. There is no disposition, certainly there is nothing to be found in the address of the right hon. the leader of the House, to indicate a disposition to withdraw from any promise that ever was made. There has been, since the promise referred to was made, a consistent readiness to live up to it, a consistent readiness to return these resources upon terms that are fair and equitable with reference to all the other provinces of the Dominion. I did not understand the hon. leader of the Opposition to take any explicit position upon the question of whether or not the other provinces had any interest in the settlement of the terms upon which these resources should be returned, but as he was at pains to point out that his acceptance of the resolution proceeded upon the assumption that the return of the resources would necessarily be made upon terms that would be fair and equitable to the other provinces, I venture to assume that he does recognize that there is an interest in the other provinces. The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat complains that this Government does not take upon itself, of its own authority, without consultation either of the provinces to whom the resources are to be returned, or of the other provinces who may be affected by the terms upon which the resources are so returned, absolutely to settle of its own authority just what are fair and equitable terms to all parties concerned, and impose them upon both classes of provinces. In that connection I think it is well to recollect that the original foundation of our present Dominion was a foundation that rested upon an agreement between the original provinces. I think it

is also fair to take it that when the con-titution of the new provinces was created, the terms then settled upon were the result of consultation, not of course with nonexistent provinces, but, as has been pointed out, on the part of the Dominion Government of the day with those provinces who at the time had the capacity to represent and to speak for the territories that were to become the provinces. The terms of those days were not imposed upon those territories until after they had been consulted, and there had been acceptance on their part.
Now a new departure means a modification of those things that were agreed to, and in the face of that, the suggestion that Parliament should take upon its(elf without any regard to the desires of or to what would be acceptable to the provinces who were to receive the resources, and without any regard to what in the judgment of the other provinces affected may be fair-to settle this matter offhand, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's suggests, seems to me a most undesirable method, a method, at all events, not to be resorted to until we are face to face with the situation where there is absolutely no other resort. We want contentment and satisfaction between the different parts of this Dominion. It is a matter of the very first importance that we should have it. We want contentment in the West with the terms and conditions upon which the resources may be returned to them, and I think therefore that it is only the part of wisdom to endeavour to ascertain what will be acceptable to those provinces even before taking up the question with the other provinces as to in what way they may consider themselves to be affected by any proposed terms, and what adjustment, if any, should be made in order to see that we maintain fairness and equality between all the provinces of this Dominion.
Taking what the hon. leader of the Opposition has said, if I understood him rightly, he thought this resolution ought to pass, for he took it for granted that our western friends in pressing for the return of the resources assumed that that return was, of course, to be made upon terms fair and equitable to all the other provinces of the Dominion. If I understood him rightly in that regard, he argued that therefore in voting for this resolution he was following out the line of policy declared by the Liberay party at its convention.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the declaration made by the Liberal party upon this subject at

the convention to which reference was made was merely the reproduction of what had been the settled and declared policy of succeeding government; ever since the Government of 1911 came into power; and we, of course, can take no exception to a reiteration of that policy. I think, therefore I shall be meeting the expressed view of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and what he assures us is the implied view of the mover of this motion, and that I may anticipate unanimity in this House, in the following motion:
That the resolution he amended by striking out all the words after the word "House" in the second line, and substituting the following therefor:
The provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted the ownership and control of the. natural resources within their respective boundaries on terms that are fair and equitable with reference to all other provinces of the Dominion.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend has omitted what perhaps will, after all, be regarded by the West as the most essential feature of the resolution, namely, the qualification that the transfer of these natural resources should be made without delay. The exception we have taken to the position of the Government as expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), is that it means a prolongation of the condition of uncertainty that exists at the present time. We agree with our western friends that this transfer should be made, but we also think that it should be made without delay. Now, if the Government is prepared to accept an amendment to the amendment by inserting, in a proper place in the resolution, the words "without further delay", I shall be prepared to accept the amendment as proposed by my right hon. friend. I certainly think that the qualifying words I suggest are a material part of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am prepared to accept those words.
Mr. SPEAKER; The resolution as now amended will read:
That, in the opinion of this House, the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted without further delay the ownership and control of the naturail resources within their respective boundaries on terms that are fair and equitable with reference to afll other provinces of the Dominion.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment to the amendment?

Carried.
Amendment to the amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the resolution as amended?
Carried.

The amendmerit as moved by the right hon. minister will have an effect similar to that of the amendment moved the other day in reference to a resolution in connection with the Hudson Bay railway; it practically makes the resolution of no effect. I am quite aware-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I trust the hon. member will bear in mind that the amendment has been adopted by the House. He will now address himself to the resolution as amended.
That is what I am doing; I presume I have the right to reply to the original motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Certainly.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that was the intention I had when I rose.
I desire to refer to some of the statements made by' the Prime Minister and others who followed him. The right hon. gentleman, in the beginning of his remarks, said that it did not lie in the mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite to express the views they had uttered; it was not consistent in them to take the stand they had taken. Now, I am not concerned with any stand that has previously been taken, rightly or wrongly, by certain hon. gentlemen on either side of the House. With me, this question has come up in the House now for the first time, and I consider that it should be decided strictly on its merits, without reference to what hon. gentlemen may or may not have done in the past. In answer to a question I asked the Prime Minister, he stated that the territories agreed to this arrangement by virtue of the fact that certain representatives from those territories wrere in the House at the time, and two names were mentioned, those of Messrs. Scott and Oliver. It may be that Messrs. Scott and Oliver considered that the arrangement made at that time was a good one from the point of view of their districts, and possibly they may be of the same opinion still; at least I am not prepared to say that they have changed their minds in any way. And as I have already pointed out, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in referring to the matter in his speech in 1914, did not, so far as I could gather, say anything in contradiction of his utterances of 1905. It is quite probable that those -who
had to do with the deal in 1905, so far as Saskatchewan and Alberta are concerned, are still of the same mind; but that is not the question now before the House. Notwithstanding the attitude taken by those gentlemen at that time, and the fact that there have been elections in Saskatchewan and Alberta since then; notwithstanding these and various other facts, the outstanding fact is that prior and subsequently to 1911, and particularly in that year, the right hon. gentleman who now represents King's (Sir Robert Borden) and who was leader of the Conservative party at that time, afterwards becoming Prime Minister, stated emphatically that these natural resources would be returned to the provinces if he were called upon to form a government. Now it is up to him, without any question whatever, it is up to the Government of which he was head, which is really the present Government, definitely to carry out the promise he then made. It looks rather strange to me, as I pointed out before, that hon. gentlemen supporting the Government should wish to defer so much to the opinions and desires of some Liberals who are not in the House now. It is something I have not observed them do to any extent during this session, or at any previous time. Or because certain gentlemen may have been inconsistent, having advocated one thing at one time and another thing now, that is no excuse for inconsistency on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Another matter that was raised is that of negotiations. The Prime Minister stated that the proposals made in this connection by the provinces were not such as could be accepted-that the letter written in 1913 which contained the proposals of the three Premiers could not receive the approval of himself or of his Government. Be that as it may, I mentioned specifically in the remarks I made earlier in the debate that the terms of that letter were simply set out as a basis for negotiation, and if not approved by the Federal Government it was then in order for the Government to submit some other proposition. I am told on good authority that after the conference of 1918, which did not result in anything, the delegates left with the distinct understanding that a definite and fair proposition would be submitted by the Minister of the Interior of that day, the present Prime Minister. I have not learned that any proposition of the kind has ever been made by the Prime Minister to the Prairie Provinces, nor have I discovered that this Gov-

ernment has ever submitted a proposal to them. The provinces on their part, as I have already pointed out, have more than once set out their case but the Prime Minister holds that the contentions were not in accordance with what the Federal Government deemed to be right, fair and equitable to the other provinces. That being so, in my opinion the Federal Government should have submitted in return a proposal which is fair and reasonable in its opinion. I submit that the Federal Government has not gone nearly as far as it should have gone, and has not done its part in this connection. It should have put forward something which it considered fair and reasonable and then if the western provinces would not accept, it would be up to them to make the next move. But as matters stand I think I am right in expressing the opinion that the next move should come from the Federal Government and it has not made any. My contention was, and is, that this matter should be settled entirely between the Dominion and the western provinces. I frankly admit that the situation is by no means a simple one, that there is perhaps no definite basis of accounting upon which to arrive at a conclusion, and there will have to be a compromise in some way. That is the reason why the provincial Premiers in the first place made their demands as they did. The Prime Minister stated to-night that the situation was so complicated and so mixed up that it would be pretty hard to arrive at anything definite, and that undoubtedly either side would likely state its case in an extreme form. But granted just for sake of argument that the provinces have set up extreme contentions, the Dominion Government has not set up any case at all, as far as I can make out, extreme or otherwise. It is therefore in order for the Dominion Government to frame a proposition and make it the basis of terms which it considers, with all the facts at its disposal, might reasonably be accepted by the provinces.
At this late hour I do not propose to make any further reply to the various Statements that have been made, other than that contained in my initial remarks. As was the case in a resolution which was moved by me earlier in the session, an amendment has been moved to the present resolution which makes it practically innocuous. The resolution as amended is not acceptable to me and is not at all satisfactory. Under the circumstances I have no other course than to ask leave to withdraw my motion.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Will the hon. member read the clause as amended.

Clause (f) of section 3 under this proposed amendment will read as follows:
If he exhibits to any of his creditors any statement of his assets and liabilities which shows that he is insolvent, or presents or causes to he presented to any such creditors a written admission of his inability to pay his debts.
Under the law as it now stands he has to exhibit to a meeting of his creditors a statement of his assets and liabilities showing he is insolvent before a receiving order can be made. The purpose of the amendment is to so change the section that if he exhibits to any of his creditors, not specially at any meeting, a statement of his assets and liabilities showing insolvency, then that is sufficient for the creditors to apply for a petition in bankruptcy.
I may state that this amendment is made at the suggestion of the judge of the Bankruptcy Court of the province of.Quebec. Under the present law it is difficult to obtain a petition in bankruptcy. A man may be insolvent to the extent that he is not able to pay one cent on the dollar, but until he exhibits a statement to his creditors at a meeting it is of no avail to secure a petition in bankruptcy. The judge of the Bankruptcy Court in Quebec, who has been sitting on these cases for the past year, was quick to see that the law is rendered nugatory if it is
	j
allowed to remain in its present form, and at his suggestion the amendment has been introduced to give the law some force.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my
suggestion in regard to this clause, and also in regard to the Bill itself, would be that as there is another amending Bill to the Bankruptcy Act now on the Order Paper, this Bill had better be allowed to stand so that all the amendments may be considered together. In the Bill of which I gave notice on Friday there are a great many amendments which will require careful consideration. The particular clause now under discussion was considered by a Special Committee of this House when the Bankruptcy Act was originally under discussion, and my recollection is that the view of the Special Committee was that it would be safer to have the clause framed as it appears to-day in the Act. A statement exhibited by a debtor at a meeting of his creditors showing insolvent circumstances is one which the whole body of creditors is made aware of at the same time. Occasionally debtors are persuaded to exhibit statements to creditors of a semi-confidential character, more often perhaps to their bankers. It was not deemed proper that these semi-confidential communications should subsequently prove to be the foundation of a petition in bankruptcy. That at all events was the view of the Special Committee. A reasonable safeguard has been provided in the section as framed in the Act, namely, that such a statement in order to be the foundation for a petition in bankruptcy should be made to a meeting of creditors and not to an individual creditor. I may be wrong and that may not be the view of the House, but I would ask my hon. friend simply to ask the committee to rise and report progress, then, when the Government measure is under consideration we will be able to have this clause fully discussed, and if it meets with the approval of the House it can be incorporated in the Government Bill. It would be more convenient in that form than any other.

I am willing to accept
the hint of the Acting Solicitor General, but before doing so I would like to point this out with regard to the section which I am now striving to amend. Suppose the debtor refuses to come before a meeting of his creditors and does not submit a statement indicating insolvency, what is to be done with him, how is he to be reached?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
A meeting of creditors
is not necessary in the first instance. All any creditor has to do is to issue a writ and secure judgment. That is an act of bankruptcy. A meeting of creditors is called as a rule to make some arrangement, to gain an extension of time, or something of that nature, and if at such a meeting the debtor admits insolvency, or makes a statement which shows insolvency, it is brought to the knowledge of all the creditors, and they or any individual creditor can act. That was considered by the Special Committee better than the method proposed in the amendment. However, there are two sides to the question, and it opens pretty broad ground for discussion. The Government has no particular view on the proposed amendment, but I think it might be very fully considered when the other Bill is brought before the House.

In the province of Quebec when suit is taken judgment sometimes is not rendered for a period ranging from six months to two years. The debtor might be hopelessly insolvent all that time and nothing could be done to throw him into insolvency. However, no good purpose is to be, served by continuing this discussion if the Acting Solicitor General is not prepared to go on with the Bill just now. Therefore I am willing to hold it in abeyance until such time as his own Bill comes up, and then this can be reintroduced.

On motion of Hon. H. S. Beland (Beauce) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend The Maple Products Act, 1920, by repealing section two of the Act and providing in lieu thereof:

1.	That no person shall manufacture for sale, keep for sale, or expose for sale or sell any article of food represented as maple sugar or maple syrup which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup.
2.	That any maple sugar or maple syrup
which is not up to the standard prescribed by the Governor in Council under the Food and Drugs Act, 1920, shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of the Food and Drugs Act, 1920.	,
3.	That the word "maple" may be used in combination with any other word or words or any letter or letters on the label or other mark, illustration or device, on a package containing any article of food resembling or being an imitation of or being a compound of maple sugar or maple syrup and other substances; and in such cases the exact proportion of maple sugar or maple syrup in such articles shall be clearly indicated on the package.

He said: Mr. Chairman, I have little to add to what I said on the introduction of a Bill with regard to this matter, when I was ruled out of order by the Speaker. The change in the law is embodied id the provision contained in paragraph 3 of the resolution, the concluding words of which are particularly important:
In such cases the exact proportion of maple sugar or maple syrup in such articles shall he clearly indicated on the package.
The object is not to prevent dealers from dealing in maple sugar or to render it more difficult for the public to get the pure article. Under the proposed amendment, when an article is offered as maple sugar or maple syrup it must be the pure article, but if for the needs of the trade it is deemed necessary to compound or to mix together maple sugar and other substances in certain proportions, that wil be permitted. In such cases, however, the exact proportion of maple sugar contained in the product shall be indicated on the package or container. It is my view that such a provision would facilitate in large measure the marketing of the pure article. If certain legislation proposed in the United States is adopted, it will be more difficult to market our maple sugar in that country. At present the manufacturers of syrup for table use are prevented by law from making a compound syrup of part maple sugar and part cane or other sugar. It is forbidden to use the word "maple" except in reference to the pure article.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says
"hear, hear," but if he was a large manufacturer of syrup for table use, he might wish to make a syrup which would contain twenty-five per cent maple sugar and seventy-five per cent cane sugar, and to sell it at a lower price than that which the pure maple sugar would command. He would market this product easily, and it would contain a proportion of maple sugar made entirely of cane sugar is acceptable, and this product would be better than the syrup containing only cane sugar, because it would contain a proportion of maple sugar. I understand that some people object to that. They do not want maple sugar to be mixed with anything at all. They may have their reasons for that; but this amendment to the present law does not preclude the marketing of pure maple syrup, and if in a window my hon. friend or any other hon. member of this House or any consumer in the counrMr A.rmstrong;.]	.

try sees an article designated as maple sugar, that must by law be the pure article. If he sees in a window an article {designated as maple ,syrup and nothing else, it must be the pure article after this resolution is adopted as before. The amendment is that it would be permissible for some dealers or manufacturers to mix the pure article with some other substances so long as they indicate on the container or the package the exact proportion of maple sugar or maple syrup in it.
What would the article be called?

It may be called whatever the dealer or manufacturer likes, but he will use the word "maple" in combination with other words. To-day no manufacturer 6f candies can offer for sale an article designated as maple cream.
Yes.

I say; no. The law, as
it is to-day, prohibits the use of the word "maple" except for the pure article. Maple cream is not pure maple sugar; it contains something else, and any dealer is absolutely prohibited, by the present law, -from offering for sale maple creams or maple candies.

The hon. gentleman has
introduced a resolution which exactly reverses the position that this House took when this whole question was discussed some years ago. The reason for placing the present legislation on the statute book is this. The country was swamped with imitations of maple syrup and maple sugar; there were "mapleine" and all kinds of articles with the word "maple" in combination and in some of the articles there was not anything in the way of maple syrup or maple sugar at all. The House came to the conclusion, on the representation of members chiefly from Quebec, (that the Act should be made so that it would be an offence for anybody to use the word "maple" in connection with any compound, and that the word "maple" could be used only in connection with pure imaple sugar and syrup. This Act was a move in the right direction. The amendment proposed simply throws the door wide open, and it will wipe out the business of maple syrup and sugar in this country, because a great deal of the maple syrup and sugar that was put on the market in the past when the door was wide open, was purely a flavouring extract that was inserted in cane sugar made out of ethers and other things, and was worse

than "squirrel" whisky, which is sold in certain parts of the country at the present time. It was not a pure article at all, and this amendment will, in my opinion, involve a great hardship to farmers who produce maple syrup and who are able to produce it now at a profit. If you open the door by this amendment, you are going back on the record. I trust the hon. gentleman who represents a constituency in which there are large manufacturers of maple syrup, will see the disadvantages to his people by the passage of this proposed legislation. I was a member of the House at the time the Act was passed, and the complaint was made to this House that the farmers could not carry on the business of making maple syrup qnd maple sugar because of the quantity of spurious imitations of various kinds put on the market. Some disreputable people would cut down maple buds, boil them in a kettle and put cane sugar in and sell the article as maple syrup because it had the faintest trace of the maple tree in it. I am strongly against the amendment; I do not think the hon. gentleman will reach it again at any rate, and the easiest way to short-cut the whole thing would be that he have the resolution dropped.

During the temporary absence of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), in order to advance his measure, I moved the first reading. I wish to say to the committee that, representing a constituency in which the people are very jealous of their reputation as manufacturers of pure maple syrup and sugar, I am opposed to this measure. The legislation introduced, I think, three years ago, was not introduced without considerable investigation and without getting the experience of experts. It was put through at the unanimous request of the representative maple sugar makers throughout Canada. It seems to me that it would be a retrograde movement at this time to adopt the principle laid down in the resolution presented by my hon. friend, and I may say to him frankly that when his Bill comes before the House, I must oppose it.

I wish to delay the House very briefly by the remarks which I have to offer in connection with this resolution. Since the resolution was placed on the Order Paper, I have had the benefit of discussing the matter with some of my constituents. I may say that the constituency Which you, Mr. Chairman, have the honour to represent, and my constituency, are possibly the foremost constituencies in the manufacture of maple syrup and maple sugar in the Dominion.
No.

That is to say, there is no finer maple syrup than the syrup produced in the constituencies of Shefford and Brome. There is good maple syrup produced elsewhere, but none better made anywhere than in the constituencies of Shefford and Brome, and the syrup and sugar made in those constituencies is beautiful, not only in its flavour, but in its appearance, and in that it has the advantage of the syrup and sugar which come from other constituencies. The feeling of those with whom I have talked the matter .over is that the Act as it at present stands is a safeguard against adulteration; thatfor years past maple sugar manufacturers and maple syrup producers have been working to create a market for a pure article. They feel that, even with the protection which my hon. friend has thrown around his Bill, this marking of the exact proportion of maple sugar syrup that is in any compound, the door may be opened to there being placed on the market and sold as maple syrup or maple sugar, as the case may be, stuff which, as a matter of fact, is not the pure product of the maple tree. Under those circumstances, I feel that I must also oppose the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland). ,
What guarantee has my hon. friend to-day that the syrup is not adulterated?
We have the Inland Revenue Department whose officers go around, I understand, testing maple syrup and determining whether or not it is the pure article.
What is to prevent the Inland Revenue Department from doing the same thing in the future?

I believe their work would be harder. The question that is placed before them now is the following: Is the maple sugar or the maple syrup a pure article? I understand that that is sometimes not always an easy question to decide, but the question which they will have to decide after this Bill passes is not only whether it is a pure article, but does it contain more or less maple sugar or maple syrup than the label shows? I understand that what my hon. friend de-

sires is that a man should have the right to make and sell a cake of let us say, 50 per cent maple sugar, 50 per cent cane sugar, so long as he marks plainly on the wrapper that it is 50 per cent, and that quantity only, of maple sugar. Now if every one was honest, if all the sugar was sold over the counter, plainly marked with the 50 per cent, there might not be so much objection, but my point is this: a wrapper may be torn off, and a cake which is only half maple sugar may be sold to an unsuspecting public as pure maple sugar. It is the same sort of thing that we do with our butter. Butter may be half butter and half oleomargarine, but we would greatly object to having butter of that sort sold as butter, even if the proportion of oleomargarine was stated upon it. I understand that we have followed the inverse method of protecting the public against the adulteration of butter by saying that oleomargarine has to be plainly marked as olemargarine before it can be sold, to differentiate it from butter. Well, here in regard to maple products we say: You cannot use the name maple unless it is the pure product. That will not prevent a man who wants to get a nice syrup which is not pure maple from getting it and selling it. He can sell it so long as he does not call it maple syrup or give the idea that it is maple syrup. I presume that he could call it Log Cabin Syrup or something of that kind, and put what flavoring of maple sugar he desired in it. I have spoken with some people of my country, ,and one especially with whom I had the privilege of discussing the matter the other day said that he was very strongly opposed to the Bill.
I also had a talk the other day with one man who has probably done as much for ' the maple sugar industry as any other man in this country. He is vitally interested in the success of that industry and he announced himself as being very much opposed to this legislation. I think on the whole the law had beter remain as it is. We have a saying in the law, that hard cases make bad laws. I understand that there has been a great slump in maple sugar, and that men who bought maple sugar all the way from 25 to 30 cents a pound last spring have a lot of the old stock still on their hands, and have to take off about 15 cents a pound in order to get rid of it. They believe that this will give them a larger market. I understand that the law as it now stands is the result of practically a unanimous request of the 
maple sugar interests, and I believe they would be opposed to any change.

I have proposed the
amendment to the present law in consequence of a very large number of petitions I have received from people in my county, thousands of them, who are interested in the maple sugar industry. Moreover, I may say that to-day there is on the market a large quantity of adulterated maple sugar and adulterated maple syiup that is called maple syrup and maple sugar and is bought for the pure article because people do not take the trouble to investigate or have it examined. The object of the amendment is to compel the man who wants to put up a mixture of maple sugar or maple syrup to state exactly what proportion of the pure product it contains. May I suggest that the resolution be reported, and that after the Bill has received its first and second readings, it be referred to the Committee on Agriculture, who may call whatever experts they desire. I will be quite willing to abide by the decision of that committee.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 80, respecting the Grand Trunk arbitration.

speakeroldname: Mr. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend if he seriously proposes to go on with the third reading of this important measure at this hour of the night?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I not only seriously propose it, but I understood the hon. member to agree the other day that we would go on with it to-day. We could have gone on with it then, but at his special request I deferred it until to-day. I might say while I am on my feet that there will be

some Senate amendments proposed. There is no important amendment affecting the substance of the Bill, unless possibly a change in the date; that would be important if it is made. There will be other amendments, however, so the Bill will come before this House again in the way that a Bill comes back from the Senate, and there will be opportunity then for discussion. Indeed, as far as that is concerned, I am not asking to curtail discussion at all now, but the hon. gentleman knows the urgency of the measure, and that I have acceded on every occasion to requests for postponement from hon. gentlemen opposite. I certainly did not expect that I would be asked again to-night to defer the third reading until to-morrow.

I quite agree with my right hon. friend that it was understood we would take up this measure on Monday; but it is now almost Tuesday. The point I wish to make is that it is unreasonable to try to discuss intelligently a measure of the importance and magnitude of this after midnight.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is only the third
reading.

Before this resolution-which extends proceedings already expensive to the taxpayers and not unremunerative to some gentlemen associated with the arbitration -is advanced further, I wish, speaking for my constituency only, to again go on record as opposed to the government operation of railways. The experience of the last few years surely has taught us that government operation of railways is neither efficient nor economical. Yet the Government at this late hour, proposes once more to stampede Canada into arbitration proceedings that will involve taking over not only railways throughout the length and breadth of Canada but railways extending into the United States. The parent system of the Grand Trunk system, as I figure, comprises 3,691 miles in Canada and there are 1,764 miles in the United States. I ask the Prime Minister what mandate he has from the people of the Dominion of Canada to go into the operation of railways in several states of the American Union? What mandate has he to take over a system of railways, of which almost one-half extends into several states of the Union? It seems to me that the Prime Minister should hesitate before forcing this measure through in the way he is doing. I am satisfied that he himself is not over confident in the success of the Government operation of railways and I repeat that representing the people of the Dominion and forgetting the interests of the Grand Trunk shareholders in England-who are quite capable of taking care of themselves-we should make haste slowly before we stampede the Dom-

inion into government operation of railways in the United States. For these reasons-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentlemen permit me a question? What authority has he for saying the Grand Trunk are quite able to take care of themselves? Is he not aware that the president has stated they are not.

Well, I take the statement of the president with a little grain of salt. I think the evidence goes to show that the Grand Trunk president is quite capable of looking after his people-he has assured them dividends on the major stocks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not on his road though.

My experience with the
Grand Trunk Railway is that he was very anxious to load this road on the people of Canada. I am not here upholding the rights of the shareholders, I am looking after the rights of the taxpayers of this country. I therefore submit to the Prime Minister that people who are called upon to pay out at this time large amounts that should go into business for the expansion of the industries of this country will not take kindly to the idea of putting their money into a venture which not only extends throughout Canada but into several states of the American Union as well. I am opposed most emphatically to this resolution.

I have
just one word to say before the vote is taken. As I said the other day I believe the Government has not been over generous in the matter of delays with the English shareholders. I believe that the Government might well have permitted a reasonable delay for the settlement of the arbitration. That is my first objection to this Bill. My other objection is that we are deciding in a very rapid way a very big issue. We are changing the management of a railway system which, during the last sixty or seventy years has accomplished a great deal for the development of Central Canada. I do not know that the shareholders and bondholders and friends of the Grand Trunk in England would not have been willing, after some delay, to reconsider the whole situation, and keep their property.
But, Mr. Speaker, my chief objection against any such venture is that which I have already expressed, much to the scandal of some good friends on both sides of the House. I am opposed to public ownership, and by this transaction we are 
adding to the already overloaded treasury of the Dominion another railway, which means for the finances of Canada and the taxpayers a very serious additional burden. I am opposed to public ownership for the following reasons: I think it is only a passing whim, and that the day is not far distant when the whole country will realize how with a light heart the Government and the people generally accepted this Populist theory of government ownership. I am opposed to government ownership because it makes for extreme delay and inertia, vacillation, hesitancy and inconsistency in matters of policy; for wasteful outlay in response to sectional demands; for insufficient provision of funds when needed for necessary purposes; for absence of close and harmonious co-operation between the legislative directorate and the executive officers. Finally, I am opposted to public ownership because it makes for insecurity of tenure in the higher places and lack of self interest as an incentive so efficiency.
I am not alone, Mr. Speaker, in that opinion. Already since this passing whim took hold of the popular imagination within the last eight or nine years I find that a good portion of our population has receded from its adhesion to that policy. But besides the man in the street who is pinched by the heavier taxation bills, and who realizes that the country will be severely mulcted by such ventures, there are men in the Government presided over by the right hon. Prime Minister who do not believe in public ownership. I dare say there is sitting in this Chamber around the right hon. gentleman colleagues whose hearts are not in this public ownership policy. I will give no names, but I will read what one of the members of the Government declared two years ago when the question came up. Sir James Lougheed, to-day Minister of the Interior, speaking on this very question used the following language:
I am not an advocate of public ownership. I simply say that this is one of the signs of the times. It is inevitable, and a duty is thrown upon the shoulders of those who represent capital and those who oppose public ownership, as well as the man in the street, in the determination of these very important questions. At the present moment, my views are these: I am in favour of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk and of any other roads that are necessary to complete a system of national transportation that will be in the interest of Canada.
And note the following words, Mr. Speaker:
But I thin]; that, while every reasonable trial should be given to public ownership, then if it

be found that public ownership cannot be advantageously carried on, the Government of Canada will be in a position to say to the capitalists of the United States and of Europe:
Observe the Ethiopian in the woodpile.
"We have a oomplete system of railways, comprising over 20,000 miles, covering the whole of this Dominion, the most complete system in the Dominion, representing engineering advantages superior possibly to those of any other system in the Dominion, and for that system we are prepared to accept offers-for its purchase or its operation or its administration."
Who said that? '

Sir James Lougheed, leader of the Government in the Senate, a member of the present Administration. Like your humble servant, he has no faith in public ownership. He is a prophet as to what the Government will eventually do with the whole system-invite capitalists from the United States or from Europe when the passing whim will have disappeared and pass the railway system over to some powerful syndicate. That is the prediction made by Sir James Lougheed, and I believe that he was simply expressing the truth, and nothing hut the truth.
I am not an expert, I am a tyro in this business, but my eyes are wide open. The taxation bill of this country is too high, the financial situation is too desperate to allow the Government to go along in any such blind fashion and throw the country into a deeper abyss. Therefore I am opposed, as is Sir James Lougheed, to public ownership. I do not want the Government to add to the already heavy burden of our taxpayers, and I do not want the Government to invite, as Sir James Lougheed predicted, capitalists from the United States or Europe to take hold of the Canadian National system. If I had my own way, Mr. Speaker, I would invite Lord Shaugh-nessy to sit with me at the council table, and I would discuss the subject with him and would accept the advice of one who is unquestionably the highest railway authority in the world to-day. But in this I pm only expressing my personal opinion. As I said a moment ago, I am but a tyro in this business, but I can see very clearly where the country is going to land if we go blindly into this railway ownership business. Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and of my hon. friend who preceded him (Mr. Robb) have induced me to say one word. Both these gentlemen have put themselves
definitely on record as being opposed to the public ownership of railways.
With Sir James Lougheed, a member of the Government supported by the hon. gentleman.

My hon. friend
expressed himself as being in complete accord with Sir James Lougheed when he said that he was opposed to the public ownership of railways, and he expressed himself as in accord with Sir James Lougheed when he suggested that the proper course to follow was to round out these systems in order that it would be possible for the Government to relieve itself of its obligations and turn them over to private ownership. Now, there is no question of public ownership or of private ownership involved in the taking over of the Grand Trunk Railway system. There is a question whether it is going to be possible for Canada to operate the railways which it now has. That is just where the matter begins and ends. Whatever the future of these railways may be, whether it be private ownership or government ownership, they cannot be operated successfully is separate entities. My hon. friend had some responsibility for bringing about the condition with which we are now faced. Does he think it would be possible for the Canadian people to retain the railways they now have and operate them successfully without eastern connections and eastern terminals? If he does not think that is possible-and I question whether he will get any railway man to suggest that it is possible-would he contend that the country should go ahead and furnish these eastern connections and eastern terminals, relieve the Grand Trunk of all its responsibility in that regard, let them keep the property they now have, go ahead as they have done, and shoulder all the responsibility on the Canadian people of taking care of the white elephant that was foisted on them by my hon. friend and his colleagues? The Grand Trunk and the Transcontinental were the genesis of our troubles and the only way we can get out of those troubles is to follow the course now being taken and link the whole combination together. As to what my hon. friend said with regard to the suggestions of Lord Shaughnessy, no one will deny that Lord Shaughnessy must be recognized as at least one of the greatest authorities on railway problems.
There are others.

Well,
there may be many others. My hon. friend's

antecedents were such as to lead us to conclude that perhaps he is an authority on railway matters. But there is nothing out of harmony with the suggestion made by Lord Shaughnessy-my hon. friend wishes to agree with him-in the taking over of the Grand Trunk railway as a prelude to any solution that may be arrived at in connection with this whole railway problem. The Grand Trunk Railway must be taken over, and the sooner it is taken over and linked up iwith the Canadian National Railways, and the sooner we shall be in a position to sit down and discuss what is to be the ultimate destiny of these railways the better. We have never yet been in a position to give them anything in the nature of an opportunity and we shall not be able to do so until all these lines are organized under one system.
Motion agreed to on division, and Bill read the third time and passed.	,
On the motion of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, the House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Tuesday.
